احتجاجات الطلاب في فرنسا مستمرة.. فماذا نعرف عنها؟. شهدت الاحتجاجات أعمال عنف واندلاع حرائق وانتشار للغاز المسيل للدموع في الشوارع وحوصرت عشرات الجامعات وتم تعليق خدمات النقل العام في عدد من المناطق.

ساكن في بلا قيود: من حق أي قارئ أن يفهم الرواية بالطريقة التي يراها.. شدّد الروائي والكاتب السوداني عبد العزيز بركة ساكن على أهمية أن يكون الكاتب ملماً بما يكتب عنه وأن تكون لديه معرفة جيدة بالمكان والزمان وشخصيات روايته.

ما يمكننا أن نتعلمه من أخطر ظاهرة "النينيو الخارق" في التاريخ. بينما يستعد العالم لما قد يكون ظاهرة نينيو غير مسبوقة، في هذا التقرير نستكشف بالرسوم المتحركة والخرائط كيفية عمل هذه الظاهرة المناخية وأهميتها.

لماذا تشعر إيران بالقلق من تعمق العلاقات بين إسرائيل والإمارات؟. زيارة رئيس الوزراء الإسرائيلي بنيامين نتنياهو إلى الإمارات تثير مخاوف إيرانية متجددة من تحول الإمارات إلى شريك أساسي في منظومة أمنية تقودها إسرائيل، رغم استمرار الروابط الاقتصادية المهمة بين طهران وأبو ظبي
"كل يوم هناك قتلى": غزيون يواجهون غارات إسرائيلية رغم وقف إطلاق النار، مع تعثر اتفاق سلام. ما يزال العديد من الفلسطينيين يعيشون في مخيمات مكتظة، في ظل تعثر الخطة الأمريكية لإنهاء الحرب إلى حد كبير.

لماذا يستهدف الحوثيون مطار الرياض في السعودية وكيف تطورت التصعيدات؟. التحالف العسكري بقيادة السعودية يعلن اعتراض وتدمير صاروخ باليستي أطلقته جماعة أنصار الله في محافظة الخرج، بعد ساعات من إعلانه سقوط مقذوف في محيط مطار الملك فهد الدولي بالدمام شرقي المملكة.
الهجوم على مطار الرياض: حدث خطير آخر في صراع مشحون بالتوتر. تصعيد الهجمات الحوثية على البنى التحتية الحيوية في السعودية يؤثر على سمعة المملكة كملاذ آمن للاستثمارات.
بريطانيا تهدد بحظر دخول الإريتريين بسبب موقف أسمرة من إعادة المهاجرين. قالت وزيرة الداخلية إنها لن تتردد في فرض إجراءات على الدول الأخرى "التي ترفض التعاون".

لماذا تحجب منظمة قرى الأطفال الدولية تقريراً عن دورها في قضية الأطفال "المخفيين" في سوريا؟. أقرّت منظمة قرى الأطفال الدولية (إس أو إس - SOS) بأن أكثر من 140 طفلاً تم نقلهم إلى مرافقها من قبل أجهزة الأمن السورية.

تقارير تفيد أن واشنطن تدرس استخدام "أم القنابل" ضد إيران إذا عاد القتال، فما حجم قوة هذا السلاح؟. نقلت شبكة "سي إن إن" عن مصادر مطلعة قولها إن الجيش يدرس الاستخدام المحتمل لقنبلة "جي بي يو-43/بي" والمعروفة باسم "أم القنابل" ضد البنية التحتية للطاقة والمواقع النووية الإيرانية.
العراق: ما السبيل لحماية النساء من التحرش والعنف الجنسي؟. كشف تحقيق أجراه فريق من بي بي سي عن شهادات صادمة من عراقيات تعرضن للتحرش الجنسي وعن معاناتهن اليومية بلا حماية قانونية فعالة.
كيف تصبح بعض عمليات رأب الجفون "وصفة لكارثة"؟. عدد مقلق من المرضى يشتكي من مضاعفات عمليات رأب جفون تجرى خارج بريطانيا بتكلفة أقل من العادة

هل يستطيع الصغار استخدام مسحوق البروتين؟. في السنوات الأخيرة، شهدت المنتجات التي تُسوَّق على أنها "عالية البروتين" انتشاراً كبيراً، بما في ذلك الحليب والزبادي والخبز والحبوب والألواح ومساحيق البروتين.

التحالف وجماعة أنصار الله يتبادلون إسقاط المسيرات، وأنباء عن قصف مدفعي سعودي على صعدة. يتبادل الطرفان إسقاط المسيرات غداة تبنّي حركة أنصار الله الحوثية هجوماً صاروخياً استهدف القصر الرئاسي في مدينة عدن

Iranians report months-long waits for unemployment benefits. Iranians receiving unemployment benefits say payments have been delayed by up to two months, leaving some struggling to pay for food and service debts, according to messages sent to Iran International.

Tehran signals escalation in conflict IRGC likens to a ‘world war’. A senior Revolutionary Guards official has compared Iran’s conflict with the United States to a world war that could reshape the global order, reflecting a mindset in Tehran that appears increasingly resistant to backing down despite the risk of renewed US attacks.

Man in Iran International attack plot told police he was paid £2,000 to film. A man accused of plotting an attack on Iran International journalists in Britain told police he had received £2,000 for filming, according to interview transcripts read at Woolwich Crown Court on Wednesday.

How Iran shielded forces over 2022 protest killings. Iran has built impunity for the killing of protesters into its laws and judicial system, Amnesty International said in an investigation detailing how security forces accused of deadly violence can help determine whether their own actions were lawful.

Ignore prices and economy is fine, Iran ex-minister says. A former Iranian labor minister has drawn ridicule after saying the country has no economic problems other than high prices and inflation, remarks that came as official data showed year-on-year inflation approaching 90%.

Shiraz and the wine industry Iran lost after 1979. Nearly five decades after the 1979 Revolution brought an end to Iran's legal wine industry, the country retains vast vineyards and a centuries-old winemaking heritage but remains absent from a global wine export market worth $37.8 billion in 2025.

Iran’s strikes on Persian Gulf water and power were deliberate - Reuters. Iran and its allies hit water plants, airports, refineries and a nuclear power station across the Persian Gulf with a precision that rules out the official story of falling debris, a Reuters investigation has found, showing the civilian damage was the aim, not a side effect.

‘We cannot bring America to its knees,’ former Tehran mayor says. Iran cannot bring the United States to its knees despite inflicting damage on American forces, a former Tehran mayor said in a state television interview, arguing that Iran's military capabilities cannot match Washington's and calling for an end to the war through negotiations.

Tehran hospital locks its main building and treats patients in the courtyard. A Social Security hospital in Tehran has locked its main building and moved treatment into a cramped clinic in its courtyard, a member of the insurer’s healthcare oversight committee said, two months after officials listed it among the capital’s unsafe hospitals.

German court jails two men over spying for Iran's Guards. A German court convicted two men of spying on prominent Jewish figures and preparing attacks against them on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guards Quds Force, sentencing both to prison on Thursday.

Armed suspect arrested over alleged plot to kill ex-minister, reformists say. An armed man was arrested over an alleged plot to assassinate a former Iranian minister after a gathering attended by Mohammad Khatami, the former president associated with efforts to reform the Islamic Republic from within, Iran’s Reform Front said.

Statement on a cyberattack targeting an Iran International correspondent. On 10 October 2026, an unauthorized third party gained access to the work account of one of our correspondents. The correspondent was approached by someone posing as a representative of an established think tank and invited to join an online meeting.

Tehran hardline mayor rolls out economic relief: is he eyeing the presidency?. Tehran’s hardline mayor Alireza Zakani has drawn accusations of using municipal resources to prepare for another presidential bid after announcing a freeze on basic food prices and payments to new parents.

US alert puts Iran’s overseas religious finance networks under scrutiny. The US Treasury’s latest warning over Iran’s alleged abuse of religious charities puts renewed attention on religious and charitable organizations outside Iran that have separately faced criminal, regulatory or government scrutiny over financial or institutional links to Tehran.

Suspect in journalist attack plot says UK-based IRGC officer threatened to kill him. A man accused of plotting an attack on Iran International journalists told a London court on Thursday that a man he identified as a Revolutionary Guards officer living in Britain threatened to kill him and his mother unless he obeyed.

Iran touts economic resilience while households struggle to afford basics. Iran’s central bank governor has dismissed claims of economic collapse, while domestic media reports describe wages failing to cover basic living costs and families struggling to afford medicines, housing and car repairs.

Iran speaker says government overstepped on anti-terror finance rules. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has ruled that part of the government’s anti-terror financing regulations violates Iranian law, saying decisions on who is designated as terrorist must remain with the Supreme National Security Council.

Iran shipped jet fuel to Myanmar despite US blockade - Reuters. Iran managed to export jet fuel to Myanmar and send several shipments of liquefied petroleum gas out of the region despite a US naval blockade that has largely halted its crude exports, Reuters reported on Friday.

Norwegian teen gets 20-year sentence in UK murder plot linked to Iran. A Norwegian teenager recruited by a Swedish crime group linked by prosecutors to the Iranian government was sentenced to 20 years’ detention in Britain on Friday.

Cameroun anglophone : le St Joseph’s College de Sasse, au cœur des luttes identitaires. Fondé en 1939 sous l’administration britannique, il a traversé les bouleversements du Cameroun anglophone, des tensions nées des indépendances aux violences de la crise séparatiste. Son histoire est celle d’une identité contestée, au cœur d’une décennie de conflit dans les régions du Nord-Ouest et du Sud-Ouest (Noso).

Pourquoi l’ouverture d’Ecobank au yuan change la donne pour le continent. En se rapprochant du système de paiement chinois (CIPS), le groupe togolais veut permettre aux entreprises africaines de régler plus directement leurs échanges avec l’Empire du Milieu. Il rejoint Standard Bank et Afreximbank dans la course aux transactions en renminbi.

Maroc : qui est Ahmed Touizi, le nouveau président de la Chambre des représentants ?. Ancré à Marrakech et dans son arrière-pays, fort de trois décennies au Parlement, le nouveau président de la première Chambre s’impose au sommet du pouvoir. Retour sur le parcours méconnu de ce vieux routier de la politique marocaine.

« N’est pas Sankara qui veut ! ». Le bilan d’Ibrahim Traoré à la tête du Burkina Faso et la nomination de Fatima-Ezzahra El Mansouri comme première femme Première ministre du Maroc sont au menu de ce Débat africain, une émission diffusée sur RFI en partenariat avec Jeune Afrique.

Niamey dénonce « un acte d’ingratitude grave » après l’expulsion de deux agents nigériens par la France. Selon une source diplomatique, Paris a déclaré persona non grata deux agents de renseignement nigériens en poste en France. La décision passe mal à Niamey, qui rappelle que l’un d’eux avait été blessé en 2014 lors d’une mission conjointe avec l’armée française.

En Côte d’Ivoire, comment Lionel Soulard est devenu l’incontournable visage de Cargill dans le cacao. Face à l’instabilité des cours du cacao, le secteur de l’or brun ivoirien, clé pour l’économie du premier producteur mondial de fèves, cherche un second souffle. Le patron de Cargill West Africa et du groupement des exportateurs appelle à un changement d’approche stratégique.

Tullow Oil : le lent effondrement d’un ex-pilier du pétrole africain. Plongé dans de graves difficultés financières, Tullow Oil replie ses ambitions africaines sur le Ghana. Fragilisée par un revers fiscal à 196,5 millions de dollars, la compagnie joue son avenir face à un État désormais en position de force.

Maroc : face à une nouvelle plainte pour faux, Rita Zniber dénonce un chantage. Frappée d’une interdiction de quitter le territoire marocain à la suite d’une plainte déposée par Mohamed Nabil Zniber, son beau-fils, la patronne du géant Diana Holding organise sa défense. Coulisses.

Remaniement en Mauritanie : pour Ghazouani, un pas de plus vers un troisième mandat ?. L’important changement gouvernemental effectué par le président mauritanien le 10 octobre a coûté son poste au ministre de l’Énergie, après l’incendie de deux postes de transformation d’électricité à Nouakchott. Mais la manœuvre s’avère bien plus politique.

Au Mali, l’armée reconnaît une bavure à demi-mot. Une frappe au Mali a fait près de dix victimes dont des femmes et des enfants, le 12 octobre. D’habitude prompte à nier les dommages collatéraux, l’armée malienne a reconnu sans précision un « incident tragique ». Est-ce le premier signe d’une reconnaissance du coût de la guerre supporté par les civils ?

Tchad-France : ce que Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno est venu négocier avec Emmanuel Macron. Après la rupture de leur partenariat militaire fin 2024, Paris et N’Djamena tentent de rebâtir leur relation sur de nouvelles bases. Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno et Emmanuel Macron excluent cependant le retour des troupes françaises sur le sol tchadien.

Affaire Martinez Zogo au Cameroun : un témoin dit subir menaces et tentatives d’influence. Un officier supérieur, témoin dans l’affaire Zogo, s’est invité au tribunal pour dénoncer des menaces pesant sur sa vie. Jeune Afrique a également pris connaissance d’un courrier d’alerte qu’il a transmis au ministre délégué à la Défense.

Cameroun anglophone : Francis Enwe, le sénateur RDPC qui parle aux séparatistes. Député puis sénateur du parti au pouvoir, cet homme d’affaires à succès vit depuis dix ans au rythme de la crise anglophone sévissant au Nord-Ouest et au Sud-Ouest (Noso). Il tente de promouvoir un dialogue avec les séparatistes, dans un pays où le pouvoir n’y est globalement pas favorable. Rencontre.

Burkina Faso : Ibrahim Traoré a-t-il confisqué l’héritage de Thomas Sankara ?. Le mémorial consacré à Thomas Sankara, érigé à Ouagadougou, change progressivement de vocation. Pensé par ses fidèles, il est aujourd’hui réinvesti par la junte dirigée par Ibrahim Traoré, qui se rêve en réincarnation du mythe révolutionnaire.

Formule 1 : le pari financier de Kagame peut-il être gagnant ?. En obtenant le retour de la F1 sur le continent, le Rwanda s’offre une vitrine internationale inédite. Et réalise un coup sportif d’envergure dont la facture financière reste un mystère.

Face à l’Éthiopie, que vaut l’armée de l’Érythrée ?. Alors que les tensions entre Asmara et Addis-Abeba ravivent le spectre d’un conflit régional, l’armée érythréenne est sous le feu des projecteurs. Quelles sont ses capacités militaires et son aptitude à tenir sur la durée ? Décryptage.

Éthiopie, Guinée, Bénin… Quels pays d’Afrique affichent la plus forte croissance économique ?. Dans son rapport sur les perspectives économiques régionales, le FMI table sur une croissance du PIB de 4,5 % en 2026 et en 2027 pour l’Afrique subsaharienne, malgré la guerre au Moyen-Orient. Une moyenne qui masque de grands écarts.

Gabon : 10 choses à savoir sur Brigitte Onkanowa, la fidèle ministre de la Défense d’Oligui Nguema. Elle est sans doute la plus discrète des membres du gouvernement gabonais, au sein duquel elle a été reconduite le 11 octobre. Générale de brigade, ex-membre du CTRI, Brigitte Onkanowa ne cesse d’affirmer sa grande loyauté au chef de l’État.

Aérien : avec la reprise de TAP, Lufthansa peut-il bousculer Air France-KLM en Afrique ?. Avec une offre de 1,2 milliard d’euros, Lufthansa intègre le capital de TAP Air Portugal. Une prise de participation qui lui ouvre grand les portes du marché lusophone en Afrique et renforce sa présence face à Air France-KLM.

En Algérie, la chute de Saïd Sayoud, ministre de l’Intérieur et coqueluche des médias. Ses propos polémiques sur le pouvoir d’achat ont scellé son sort mais le ministre, rétrogradé le 13 octobre, paie aussi sa mauvaise gestion des incendies de l’été. Une chute brutale pour un homme qui semblait promis aux plus hautes responsabilités.

Rançons, zakat, territoire : pourquoi la guerre entre le Jnim et l’État islamique s’intensifie au Sahel. Le 10 octobre, de sanglants combats ont opposé le Jnim à l’État islamique au Burkina Faso. Un nouvel épisode dans la rivalité entre les deux groupes jihadistes, sur fond de volonté d’extension et de contrôle des financements, qui menace désormais de déborder au-delà du Sahel.

Carburant de la police : au Cameroun, ce que l’on sait du scandale qui menace Martin Mbarga Nguélé. Le Tribunal criminel spécial enquête sur un présumé détournement de dizaines de milliards de F CFA de carburant par la DGSN. Alors qu’une quarantaine de policiers sont sous les verrous, l’enquête pourrait remonter jusqu’au sommet.

Cameroun anglophone : dix ans après la marche des avocats, un système judiciaire toujours en crise. Dix ans après les manifestations d’avocats anglophones, les revendications initiales ont été largement éclipsées par la lutte indépendantiste et les violences. Si Yaoundé a pris des mesures pour répondre aux griefs, leur mise en œuvre reste incomplète.

Au Maroc, l’opposition comme horizon politique pour le PJD. Laminé en 2021, le parti islamiste a retrouvé une partie de son électorat en 2026, ce qui devrait lui permettre de peser dans les débats tout en restant loin de la coalition au pouvoir. Encore lui faudra-t-il sortir d’une posture limitée à la contestation.

Cacao : pourquoi l’alliance entre la Côte d’Ivoire et le Ghana vacille. L’association nouée en 2018 entre Abidjan et Accra pour peser sur le marché mondial du cacao montre des signes d’essoufflement. Ce tandem vacille alors que les deux pays sont sous pression pour renforcer la traçabilité de leurs fèves.

Au Sénégal, pourquoi Pastef se heurte à répétition à la censure du Conseil constitutionnel. Depuis les législatives de 2024, pas moins de dix textes de loi émanant du parti d’Ousmane Sonko ont été censurés par les « sages ». Décryptage d’un bras de fer institutionnel qui vient encore de rebondir.

En Centrafrique, qui sont les activistes arrêtés après la journée ville morte ?. Cinq responsables de la société civile centrafricaine ont été arrêtés le 15 octobre à Bangui, alors qu’ils s’apprêtaient à s’exprimer sur les suites du mouvement contre la vie chère. L’opposition dénonce une atteinte à l’État de droit.

Cameroun : Samuel Mvondo Ayolo dément de nouvelles rumeurs sur la mort de Paul Biya. Une rumeur annonçant la mort du président Biya a circulé sur les réseaux sociaux. Contacté par Jeune Afrique, Samuel Mvondo Ayolo, le directeur du cabinet civil de la présidence, dément.

Souleymane Diarrassouba : « Avec son nouveau Plan national de développement, la Côte d’Ivoire change d’échelle ». Industrialisation, TGV, recul de la pauvreté : le PND 2026-2030 de la Côte d’Ivoire voit grand. Et le ministre chargé de sa concrétisation défend un programme de 175 milliards d’euros, dont le succès repose largement sur les investisseurs privés.

RDC : ce que l’on sait des perquisitions visant l’entourage de Félix Tshisekedi en Belgique. Plusieurs perquisitions ont été menées en Belgique mercredi 14 octobre, en lien avec une plainte déposée en 2025 contre neuf personnes proches du président congolais. Cette procédure fragilise la relation congolo-belge.

Au Niger, une éruption de pétrole provoque un incident environnemental « d’une gravité exceptionnelle ». D’importantes quantités de pétrole brut et de gaz sont projetées à plus de dix mètres de hauteur, ont expliqué les autorités. Les causes de l’incident, qui a commencé le 25 septembre dans l’est désertique du pays, « ne sont pas encore totalement établies », mais la « piste criminelle ou terroriste » est écartée.

En Libye orientale, l’ascension fragile de Saddam Haftar, le fils du maréchal. Saddam Haftar, le dirigeant de la Cyrénaïque, est parvenu à prendre le contrôle du Parlement de Benghazi début octobre, consolidant ainsi son pouvoir et renforçant son statut de successeur de son père. Non sans attiser des querelles fratricides au sein de son clan.

Images. L’annonce surprise de la création d’un nouveau mouvement politico-militaire en République démocratique du Congo. Joseph Kaliba préside dorénavant le Front pour la refondation de la nation (FRN), une alliance avec les groupes rebelles AFC et M23.

Au Nigeria, le milliardaire Aliko Dangote veut faire de l’entrée en Bourse de sa raffinerie de Lagos une opération populaire. Le magnat nigérian des affaires a promis que l’entrée sur la place financière de Lagos de sa raffinerie serait « l’introduction en Bourse du peuple ». Il ambitionne de rassembler 10 millions de souscripteurs.

La formule 1 retourne en Afrique pour la première fois depuis 1993, avec dix ans de Grand Prix au Rwanda « au début des années 2030 ». La formule 1 a officialisé, mardi, sa venue au Rwanda à compter du début de la prochaine décennie. La discipline n’était pas venue sur le continent africain depuis 1993 et le Grand Prix de Kyalami, en Afrique du Sud.

A Paris, Emmanuel Macron et Mahamat Idriss Déby actent le renouveau de leur coopération militaire. Après la brouille provoquée par l’éviction de l’armée française du Tchad, les deux chefs d’Etat se sont rapprochés au cours de l’année écoulée. L’armée française reprend même discrètement pied dans son bastion historique.

Ceuta est « indissociable » de l’Espagne, déclare Felipe VI, en visite historique dans l’enclave. Le roi d’Espagne a affirmé la souveraineté « indiscutable » de l’Espagne sur Ceuta lors d’une visite historique mardi dans l’enclave du nord de l’Afrique, revendiquée par le Maroc.

En RDC, l’ancien président Joseph Kabila prend la tête des rebelles de l’Est. Le nouveau Front pour la refondation de la nation, dirigé par l’ex-chef de l’Etat, dénonce la « tyrannie » de l’actuel président congolais, Félix Tshisekedi.
Niger : les images d’une éruption de pétrole qui provoque l’inquiétude. Selon le ministère du pétrole, il s’agit d’un « incident environnemental d’une gravité exceptionnelle ».

Au Liberia, la création de plus en plus incertaine d’un tribunal pour juger les crimes de guerre. Plus de deux décennies après la fin d’une période de guerres civiles qui a fait 250 000 morts, aucune personne impliquée dans les conflits n’a été jugée au Liberia.

Pour la « gen Z » de Madagascar, un an après le putsch militaire, les lendemains qui déchantent. « Madagascar, un an après le coup d’Etat » (1/4). Lancé en septembre 2025, le mouvement de protestation de la jeunesse malgache, qui a conduit au renversement du président Andry Rajoelina, se heurte aux promesses d’une « refondation » du pouvoir par la junte restée lettre morte.

Le Maroc désapprouve en silence la visite du roi d’Espagne, Felipe VI, à Ceuta et à Melilla. Mohammed VI n’a pas publiquement condamné le déplacement du monarque espagnol dans les enclaves d’Afrique du Nord, mais les signes du mécontentement royal sont là.

A l’île Maurice, un couvre-feu décrété après plusieurs jours de manifestations et de violences, déclenchées par un tir policier. Un policier a grièvement blessé par balle une femme, vendredi, à Camp-Levieux, au sud de Port-Louis. Selon la police, 84 personnes ont été interpellées mardi. Les faits recensés comprennent des pillages, des incendies, des actes de violence et des infractions au couvre-feu.

Navanethem Pillay, Prix Nobel de la paix : sur Gaza, « on nous a accusés d’antisémitisme et de partialité. Mais je sais ce qui est constitutif du crime de génocide ». La juriste sud-africaine a présidé la commission d’enquête du Haut-Commissariat des Nations unies aux droits de l’homme, qui a estimé qu’un génocide se déroulait à Gaza. Dans un entretien au « Monde », elle revient sur son travail, récompensé le 9 octobre par le prix Nobel de la paix.

« Les Damnés de la donnée » : les travailleurs du Sud, invisibilisés et pourtant indispensables au développement de l’IA. Au fil d’une enquête menée auprès d’annotateurs de données à Madagascar, le sociologue Clément Le Ludec met en lumière la centralité du travail de cette main-d’œuvre précarisée et invisibilisée, indispensable au bon fonctionnement des systèmes d’intelligence artificielle.

Ceuta : des ONG accusent l’armée espagnole de « cruauté » à l’égard des migrants et dénoncent le non-respect de leurs droits fondamentaux. Au moment où le roi Felipe VI visitait la ville nord-africaine, mardi, huit ONG ont annoncé la saisine du défenseur du peuple espagnol pour dénoncer l’opacité entourant les retours prétendument volontaires vers le Maroc.

A Madagascar, l’ascension de l’ambitieux colonel Michaël Randrianirina. « Madagascar, un an après le coup d’Etat » (2/4). Depuis son arrivée au pouvoir, le « colonel Michaël » tente de rassurer ses partenaires et multiplie les promesses aux Malgaches, dans l’optique du scrutin présidentiel attendu d’ici à novembre 2027. Des observateurs indépendants alertent toutefois sur une opposition et une justice muselées.

Huit ans après la sortie de « Rafiki », la Cour suprême kényane se prononce sur l’interdiction du film pour « promotion du lesbianisme ». Le long-métrage, qui raconte l’histoire d’amour de deux jeunes femmes à Nairobi, n’avait été autorisé en 2018 que pendant une seule semaine sur décision de justice et avait battu des records au box-office.

En Ethiopie, la fête ancestrale d’Irreecha connaît un regain de popularité après des décennies de répression. Longtemps caisse de résonance de la résistance du peuple oromo contre le pouvoir, le rassemblement culturel est désormais mis en avant par le gouvernement comme un symbole de renouveau national.

Ethiopie : au Tigré, une administration intérimaire mise en place par le gouvernement fédéral. La région, en proie aux combats depuis plusieurs semaines, était dirigée jusque-là par les rebelles du Front de libération du peuple du Tigré.

Pakistan stands shoulder to shoulder with Saudi Arabia. The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia is confronting a grave assault on its security as the Houthi militia unleashes relentless missile and drone attacks on its cities, civilian infrastructure and vital economic facilities. Innocent lives have been lost, families placed in danger and daily life disrupted. These attacks flagrantly violate the Kingdom’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, threatening peace and stability across the region. For Pakistan, the position has been clear, consistent and unequivo

Israel killed my father and brother. A year after the 'ceasefire', I cannot reach their graves Submitted by Mona Ramadan on Tue, 10/13/2026 - 07:16 Israel's expanding Yellow Line swallows more of Gaza as hospitals are forced to close and displaced families face another winter in worn-out tents A Palestinian boy stands beside a concrete block marking Israel’s so-called Yellow Line in the east of Deir al-Balah, central Gaza, on 22 July 2026 (Eyad Baba/AFP) Off Before the start of the genocide in Gaza , I lived in Beit Lahia in the north. My house was destroyed in an Israeli air strike that killed my father and my brother. They are still buried beneath the rubble of my home. We have not been able to give them a proper burial. Today, I am displaced with my family in Deir al-Balah, in central Gaza. When Palestinians were allowed to return to the north of Gaza in January 2025, following the second "ceasefire", I went back to Beit Lahia. I walked around 13km to get there, because something inside me told me I might never get another chance to see my home. I arrived with bleeding feet. I did not care. I just wanted to see it with my own eyes, because I knew it might be the last time. It was. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); A year on from the third so-called "ceasefire", which began on 10 October 2025, almost nothing has improved for the population here, including my own family. People still live in worn-out tents and struggle to meet their most basic needs. They are still carrying immense grief and loss. People continue to lose their loved ones in different ways: through bombs and through the destruction left behind, when buildings damaged in Israeli attacks collapse on the people sheltering inside them, sometimes while they are asleep. The atrocities do not stop there. Our land is being taken from us. The " Yellow Line " that Israeli forces have drawn around us is moving further every day - 10 metres here, 100 metres there, as if no one is watching. We are watching. Everything beyond the Line A short time ago, my family received the news that the Yellow Line of Israeli military control had advanced further into Beit Lahia, beyond the rubble of our home. It has become impossible even to look at the area without risking being targeted or shot at by the Israeli military. We heard this news and immediately thought of the people buried beneath the rubble of our home: my father and my brother. Killing them was not enough. Their graves have now been erased, just like everything else beyond the Line. I, like many people in Gaza, have had to search for what is left of my home through satellite imagery, and it feels like losing my father and brother once again. To me, the word 'yellow' has come to mean everything left behind the Line: homes and neighbourhoods that remain deserted, emptied, erased To me, the word "yellow" has come to mean everything left behind the Line: homes and neighbourhoods that remain deserted, emptied, erased. We see what is being destroyed, and we know that erasing the evidence does not erase what happened. We are still here. We witnessed it. We remember. My home was between two hospitals: the Indonesian Hospital and Kamal Adwan Hospital. The Indonesian Hospital stands empty , shut down by Israeli troops in June 2025, and the Israeli military has built a base beside it. Kamal Adwan Hospital, meanwhile, now sits around 150 metres from the Yellow Line. One of northern Gaza's few remaining hospitals, it has been repeatedly attacked and forced to suspend its services, including in September. As a humanitarian, I have seen up close how this ongoing genocide is affecting people's health and their access to healthcare. I have seen premature babies born with complications in hospitals struggling with constant shortages. I have seen doctors doing everything they can to save lives. I have seen the fear and hope in mothers' eyes as they bring their children in for treatment. Wherever I go, I leave with a heavy heart. I cannot imagine what local health workers must be carrying on their shoulders every single day. They are exhausted and grieving, and yet still show up for their patients. My colleagues and I at Medical Aid for Palestinians ( MAP ) stand alongside them and support them with the resources we have. We will not back down. We cannot leave them to face all of this alone. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Another winter in tents The summer heat has passed, but winter is on the way. Hundreds of thousands of people living in makeshift shelters across Gaza are going to face another harsh winter. These tents are already worn out and cannot withstand the storms to come. With roads and infrastructure destroyed, rainwater will collect around the tents, adding even more to people's suffering. No human being should have to live through what people in Gaza have been living through. No one should have to spend years without safety, without a home, without access to the healthcare they need and without knowing what tomorrow will bring. For Gaza's orphans, the safety of childhood vanished with their parents Read More » When it comes to children, the cost is even harder to put into words. They deserve to be born safely and to get medical care when they need it. They deserve to sleep without fear, to grow up happily and to have a future they can look forward to. After three years, I feel like I am repeating myself, but I will keep saying these things for as long as people are forced to live like this. These are not impossible demands. We are asking for the most basic things: safety, dignity, healthcare and the chance to live. Until that becomes a reality, I will keep on repeating myself. What has happened in Gaza cannot simply be erased. You can destroy homes, hospitals, streets and entire neighbourhoods. You can erase places from the map. You cannot erase what happened to the people who lived there. We carry it with us. We remember every loss, every displacement, every moment we were forced to endure. We will carry those memories for the rest of our lives. I keep asking myself: how much more does the world need to see? How many more lives have to be shattered before words become action? We have heard enough statements. People in Gaza do not need another promise. We need action. We need our rights to be respected. We need this daily suffering to end. We need safety, dignity and healthcare. We need homes we can return to and the chance to build a future. After everything we have lost, we should not have to keep asking for the right to live. The Rohingya case that could redefine the law on genocide Submitted by Sondos Asem on Fri, 10/16/2026 - 08:00 Judges in the Gambia v Myanmar case are preparing a ruling that will have ramifications for Israel and Gaza In the first week of September 2017, Antonia Mulvey was on the Bangladesh-Myanmar border, interviewing women and children who had fled across it days earlier. “Women waited all day to talk to me and they'd had horrific things happen to them,” she told Middle East Eye. “What struck me when I listened to their stories was that they were asking me for justice.” Mulvey was one of the first three investigators deployed by a UN fact-finding mission . Her brief was sexual violence and crimes against children. Nine years later, the case that grew out of those accounts is nearing its end, with the International Court of Justice (ICJ) expected to rule in the coming weeks on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. Mulvey, now executive director of Legal Action Worldwide (LAW), which represents Rohingya witnesses in the case, said that if the judges rule against Myanmar, it will be the first time the court has found a state responsible for committing genocide. For many Rohingya, the ruling is about more than the past. “We need to fix the root cause,” one refugee told LAW researchers. “The best justice for us is to fix the root cause of the problem.” Legal experts say they also expect the outcome to have consequences for other ICJ cases involving allegations of genocide, most pressingly South Africa's case against Israel over its war against Palestinians in Gaza, where the confirmed death toll has reached almost 75,000 people. Michael Becker, a professor of international law at Trinity College Dublin, described the case as a "crucial opportunity for the ICJ to clarify and develop the law on genocide” which, he said, would have "major repercussions" for the South African case. Decades of persecution The Rohingya, a mostly Muslim minority, have lived for generations in western Myanmar’s Rakhine State. Northern Rakhine was the only part of the country where they formed a majority. Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law left the Rohingya off the list of the country's officially recognised ethnic groups, leaving most of them stateless. The state and its lawyers refer to the Rohingya as “Bengalis”, a term that casts them as migrants from Bangladesh. For decades, restrictions on the Rohingya’s movement, marriage rights, education and access to healthcare have been documented. Hundreds of thousands fled to Bangladesh in waves of violence in 1978, and again in 1991 and 1992. In this photograph taken on 7 September 2017, unidentified men carry knives and slingshots near Maungdaw in Rakhine state (AFP) In 2012, clashes in Rakhine displaced about 140,000 people, most of them Rohingya. Many remain confined to camps around the state capital, Sittwe. “Rohingya have been persecuted in Myanmar for decades,” said Salma, a Rohingya survivor who attended the ICJ hearings in January, in comments shared by LAW. She asked that only her first name be used. For many refugees, justice now means one thing above all: citizenship. In a survey conducted by LAW of just under 500 refugees in the Cox's Bazar camps in Bangladesh, 86 percent of participants said citizenship and the right to identify as Rohingya were necessary for justice. “We want [the] international community to destroy the 1982 law, and we hope they will do it,” one participant said. “We had Myanmar citizenship, and we were living there for a long time, and our citizenship should be restored. If they provide these two things, we will get everything.” “They want justice, but they want citizenship,” Mulvey said. “They want to be acknowledged for what happened, and they want that land and property back.” 'Clearance operations' On 25 August 2017, Myanmar's military launched what it called “clearance operations” in northern Rakhine State, after the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) attacked police posts. More than 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh in the months that followed. About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in the camps of Cox's Bazar. In 2018, the UN fact-finding mission concluded that there was enough information to infer genocidal intent. It called for senior generals - including then-army chief Min Aung Hlaing, who is now president - to be investigated and prosecuted. Mulvey said she drafted the report's sections on sexual violence and crimes against children. “It was the UN fact-finding mission report that Gambia relied upon in order to initiate proceedings at the ICJ,” she said. A Rohingya man passes a child through a barbed wire border fence near Maungdaw on the border with Bangladesh on 28 August 2017 (AFP) Abubacarr Tambadou, the Gambia's then justice minister, had spent years as a prosecutor at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. He visited the Cox's Bazar camps in 2018. In November 2019, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, the Gambia filed its case. The West African country had no direct link to the violence. It relied on the principle, accepted by the court in 2022, that every state party to the 1948 Genocide Convention has a common interest in seeing it upheld. In January 2020, the court unanimously ordered Myanmar to take all measures within its power to prevent genocidal acts. A year later, the military seized power. In July 2022, the judges rejected Myanmar's objections to the court's jurisdiction, clearing the way for the hearings that took place in January this year. 'It was very silent' Over three weeks of hearings, the court heard from three Rohingya witnesses in closed session: two men and a woman. They were identified in court only by their initials, and each came from one of three villages at the centre of The Gambia's case: Min Gyi, Maung Nu and Chut Pyin. Mulvey, their lawyer, said they spoke about the killing of their family members, the sexual violence they had been subjected to and their flight from Rakhine. Two travelled to the Hague from Cox's Bazar and one from Canada, where they had been resettled. “It was very silent. You could also hear crying. It was extraordinarily powerful testimony,” Mulvey said. “Of course we have to wait to see what the judgment is, but you could feel the weight of it.” LAW also brought a victims' delegation of three Rohingya survivors to sit in the courtroom: a man, a woman and a hijra, a term used in South Asia for transgender and intersex people. Mulvey said it was the first time a transgender survivor had been part of a delegation in the court. “We did not know that legal proceedings existed, and we could fight for our rights,” Salma, who part of the delegation, said. “But this time, we have the tools to defend ourselves and demand accountability and reparation for what happened to us.” Rehana, the delegation's hijra member, who also asked to be identified by her first name only, said she hoped a ruling would include the whole community. “If the genocide is recognised, we hope that we will be getting our justice. Justice for our entire community, including hijra,” she said. LAW also submitted hundreds of pages of written witness evidence, which Mulvey said The Gambia relied on heavily. Rape and sexual violence were central to The Gambia's case. “They selected, particularly, women and girls of reproductive age. They gang raped them. That was the method of choice,” Mulvey said, of army soldiers. She said investigators found “a pattern of biting, to leave an indelible mark on them”. She said rape in front of the community reflected “the intent to destroy the very social fabric of the community”. The ICJ has accepted before that rape can be an act of genocide, in Bosnia v Serbia and Croatia v Serbia. But in neither case did it find the intent required to classify those acts as genocide. A ruling against Myanmar on this point would mark “the first time the ICJ has actually found sexual violence itself to constitute genocide in a merits judgment”, Mulvey said. What is genocide? In deciding the case, the judges will draw on the Genocide Convention itself, the court’s own earlier rulings, and the case law of the international criminal tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda. Israel’s war on Gaza: What is the meaning of genocide? Read More » The Genocide Convention, adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948, defines genocide as any of five acts “committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such”. In Bosnia v Serbia in 2007, the court held that the intent must be to destroy at least a substantial part of the group, and that it must be physical or biological destruction rather than cultural destruction. It also ruled that charges of such exceptional gravity against a state must be proved by evidence that is “fully conclusive”. Intent can be shown by “particular circumstances” or inferred from a pattern of conduct. But in Croatia v Serbia in 2015, the court set a high bar for inference. To infer genocidal intent from a pattern of conduct, it said, “it is necessary and sufficient that this is the only inference that could reasonably be drawn from the acts in question”. Furthermore, applying those tests, the court found in the Bosnia v Serbia case in 2007 that genocide had been committed only at Srebrenica, and that Serbia was responsible for failing to prevent and punish it, not for committing it. The Gambia's case Philippe Sands and Paul Reichler, two lawyers representing the Gambia, argued that Myanmar’s military operations in northern Rakhine State targeted a substantial part of the Rohingya population and that the evidence pointed to an intent to destroy the group. Sands used Myanmar's own figures from its written pleadings to address whether Myanmar had targeted a “substantial” part of the Rohingya. 'They selected, particularly, women and girls of reproductive age. They gang raped them. That was the method of choice' - Antonia Mulvey, lawyer He calculated that 815,459 Rohingya lived in northern Rakhine's three townships, Maungdaw, Buthidaung and Rathedaung, before the 2017 operations. About 700,000 of them, nearly nine in 10, fled to Bangladesh. The military “targeted tens of thousands of homes, and over 800,000 human beings”, Sands said. Myanmar had argued that the estimated 10,000 to 25,000 people killed did not amount to a substantial part of the group. Sands said those figures were “likely to be an underestimate”. Myanmar “has gone out of its way to destroy the evidence, including the evidence of the burial of large numbers of bodies in mass graves”, he said. “Genocide is not a numbers game,” Sands said, explaining that “there is no magical number of victims which turns one kind of crime into another kind of crime.” “The 700,000 who fled to Bangladesh for their lives were no less targeted than their murdered brothers and sisters,” the British lawyer said. Gambia's lawyers Philippe Sands and Paul Reicher, and the Agent of The Gambia, Abubacarr Marie Tambadou, on the first day of the hearings, Tuesday 10 December 2019 (UN Photo/ICJ/Frank van Beek) Sands also argued that northern Rakhine mattered because it was the one region where Rohingya were the majority. Turning to intent, he said that it was proved both by “particular circumstances” and by a pattern of conduct. He pointed first to the three witnesses' villages. “There is no world in which the shooting of Witness MS's daughter, as she waded across a river to escape, was not genocidal; or the intentional burning of his wife and four other children inside a house,” Sands told the court. “There is no world in which the gang rape of Witness NJ, the murder of her infant child in front of her, was not genocidal.” Myanmar acted with genocidal intent, Sands said, because “its discriminatory policies, its hate speech, its pre-planning and organisation, its extreme brutality, its sexual violence, its targeting of children, its destruction of evidence, its impunity for the perpetrators, its failure to co-operate with the UN, cannot reasonably be understood in any other way”. The counter-terrorism defence Reichler addressed what is known as the “only reasonable inference” test, which in this case would require proving whether any explanation other than genocide could reasonably account for what happened in Rakhine. Myanmar's answer was counter-terrorism. “They have put all their eggs in the counter-terrorism basket,” Reichler said. He told the court that Myanmar's lead counsel, Christopher Staker, had conceded that genocide can take place during a counter-terrorism operation. Even if Myanmar was responding to Arsa, he argued, “the fact that there was a counter-terrorism operation in progress … is pure context. It is not intent.” The question, Reichler said, was what the state intended “at the time its authorised agents began firing their weapons deliberately at Rohingya civilians, including women and children”. (L-R) Monaira, a hijra survivor, Yousuf, a Rohingya, lawyer Antonia Mulvey, and Salma, pictured outside the ICJ building in the Hague in January 2026 (LAW/Antoine Guibert) Reichler then dealt with the other possible explanation: that Myanmar meant to drive the Rohingya out, not destroy them. That was the conclusion the court reached about Serbia and Croatia in 2015. Reichler cited the testimony of the Gambia’s military expert, who was asked whether the operations could have been ethnic cleansing, rather than genocide. The expert said they could not, because ethnic cleansing does not involve killing a group’s children. He added that a force seeking only to drive a population out would not keep shooting at people as they fled, or station troops on the river to sink their boats as they were about to reach Bangladesh. Soldiers also laid landmines at border crossings after 25 August 2017. The fact finding mission said this showed the mines were “intended to target fleeing Rohingya civilians and to prevent those who had already left from returning”. Russia, Georgia and forced displacement Reichler contrasted Rakhine with Georgia v Russia, a case in which he had acted for Georgia. In this case, Russian forces ordered ethnic Georgians to leave South Ossetia. Those who complied were not harmed. Fleeing refugees were not shot at and there was no systematic sexual violence. “On those facts, if proven, this was forced displacement, or ethnic cleansing. It was not genocide,” Reichler said. The wars in the former Yugoslavia were “essentially about the control of territory,” he argued. The Tatmadaw, Myanmar's military, “were not seeking to enlarge Myanmar's territory”. He warned that Myanmar might “change its narrative in the second round , after we have finished speaking and there is no opportunity for us to respond further”. Mulvey said that is what happened. Myanmar “did not argue deportation or forcible transfer until the very end of their oral hearings”, she told MEE. In Myanmar’s final session on 29 January, counsel Stefan Talmon quoted one of The Gambia’s own witnesses, identified as MN, telling the court: “We knew that the military did this to force us out of the country.” From such accounts, Talmon argued, the court could conclude that “the intention of the military was not to destroy them as a people as such but to force them out of the country”. “There is thus at least one other inference that can reasonably be drawn from the conduct,” he said. Srebrenica genocide survivors draw parallels with Gaza 30 years after massacre Read More » But even if expulsion had been the aim, Reichler argued that the court's own judgments allowed for a genocide finding if the displacement was carried out “with a view to the destruction of the group, as distinct from its removal from the region”. Reichler argued that other motives, such as fighting Arsa, would not rule out genocidal intent. He noted that in Bosnia the court found genocide at Srebrenica even though the Bosnian Serb leadership's “essential motive” was to create a larger Serb state. What mattered was the intent at the moment Myanmar soldiers were “segregating and executing men and boys, raping and gang raping women and girls, killing children and infants – tossing them into fires”. He said the destruction continued well into 2018, including in more than 180 villages where Myanmar admits there was no Arsa activity, and was followed by bulldozing, resettlement by ethnic Rakhine and the building of military bases. Mulvey described the same pattern from her own investigations. “They would surround the village. Then often in the early hours of the morning when people were asleep, they would fire mortars into the village. They would then proceed by shooting indiscriminately at civilians,” she told MEE. She said soldiers continued to shoot at people as they fled towards Bangladesh. “What they did was to ensure that they were killed along the way,” she said. Myanmar rejected all the allegations. It argued that the operations were a lawful response to attacks by Arsa. What western nations argued In November 2023, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands and the UK filed a joint submission to the court in support of the Gambia. They were among 11 states that intervened in the case. States that intervene in this way do not comment on the facts, only on how the Genocide Convention should be read. The six states warned that the “only reasonable inference” test should not be applied so strictly that genocide becomes “near-impossible” to prove, since states rarely put an intent to destroy a group in writing. Rohingya refugees hold paintings during the 'Genocide Remembrance Day' rally to mark the anniversary of their mass exodus from Myanmar following a military crackdown (AFP) They also argued that the number of people killed should not decide whether genocide took place. Rape, sexual violence and the targeting of children serve no military purpose, so such acts can point strongly to an intent to destroy a group, they wrote. The six states added that UN fact-finding reports deserve particular weight as the work of independent investigators. Both Sands and Reichler cited the submission in their closing arguments. 'Major repercussions for Israel case' Becker, a professor of international law at Trinity College Dublin, said this was the first time a court would rule on mass human rights violations in a case brought by “a non-injured state acting to uphold international law”. “Cases like The Gambia v Myanmar have arguably sought to transform the role and function of the ICJ in contemporary affairs. The outcome here may determine whether that trend will continue,” Becker told MEE. 'Whether the ICJ accepts or rejects that view of genocidal intent will have major repercussions for South Africa's case against Israel' - Michael Becker, law professor He said the judgment would be “a crucial opportunity for the ICJ to clarify and develop the law on genocide”, particularly on how intent can be established by inference. “The core of Myanmar's argument is that actions that can reasonably be characterised as a counter-terrorism operation cannot simultaneously be treated as acts of genocide,” he said. "Whether the ICJ accepts or rejects that view of genocidal intent will have major repercussions for South Africa's case against Israel at the ICJ," Becker explained, "where Israel has similarly claimed that an armed conflict with Hamas precludes a finding that Israel has simultaneously undertaken actions aimed at the physical destruction of the Palestinian population of Gaza.” Becker said “recent claims that the ICJ may end up 'lowering the standard' to establish genocidal intent are misguided because they fail to acknowledge the ambiguities in the ICJ's pronouncements on genocidal intent”. He added that the ruling would show how the court treats cases built largely on UN inquiry reports. Myanmar made attacks on the reliability of the fact-finding mission’s reports a central part of its defence, while the Gambia relied on the same reports extensively. “If the ICJ shows a reluctance to credit the findings of such reports, this will send a strong signal to South Africa, and potential litigants in other future cases, about the need to find other ways to support their claims,” he said. A major UN inquiry last year already concluded that Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza. Its chief investigator, Navi Pillay , told MEE at the time that her report used the same legal standard used by the ICJ in determining a finding of genocide and that it would "bear particular probative value and can be relied upon" by the court. Israel submitted its response to South Africa's case in March. South Africa's reply is due in November 2027. What the victims want Mulvey said she is often asked what a ruling would mean for people in Cox's Bazar “who barely have $1 a day”. “The short answer is yes, it makes a difference to the community,” she said. “It's important for them that the world's highest court recognises what happened to them.” Many refugees told LAW researchers that compensation and punishment alone would not be enough. “What is the reason for the issue that happened to us? We need to fix the root cause,” one participant in the survey said. “If we want compensation, their punishment, and such things, I don't think we get our justice. 'For me, justice means truth. It means that perpetrators must be held accountable' - Samir Sadaf, young Rohingya “Justice [meaning citizenship] is important for our children and grandchildren,” one woman who took part in the survey said. “If it prevails, they will have access to education and they will be able to become successful… in Myanmar.” The Gambia's final submissions reflected some of these demands. It asked the court to order Myanmar to prosecute those responsible and to provide reparations to the victims. These include safe and dignified return, the restoration of property, the right to identify as Rohingya, and “full and equal citizenship”. LAW has called for a trust fund for the Rohingya that would be linked to any reparations the court orders. Samir Sadaf, a young Rohingya man who fled Rakhine as a child, described what justice would mean beyond a court ruling. “For me, justice means truth. It means that perpetrators must be held accountable,” he wrote in an article published by LAW. “Where there is justice, there should be safety, equal rights, freedom of movement, and dignity.” Enforcing the law ICJ judgments are binding and cannot be appealed, but the court has no means of enforcing them. If a state refuses to comply, the matter can go to the UN Security Council, where China and Russia , both partners of Myanmar's military government, hold vetoes. Min Aung Hlaing, who led the 2017 operations, named himself president in April after contested elections. “While it may prove impossible to enforce such a judgment while Myanmar continues to operate under military rule, compliance with the ICJ judgment may become the price of readmission to the international community,” Becker said. A ruling that Myanmar breached the convention “can also increase the pressure on third states to disengage from Myanmar until it demonstrates genuine reform”, he said. Mulvey said LAW's victims' delegation will be in the courtroom when the judgment is read. Salma, who sat in the court through the January hearings, said the Rohingya would not give up. “We won't go back without justice,” she said. UK Green motion on Zionism: Why we need to change the conversation Submitted by Ben Jamal on Wed, 10/14/2026 - 22:17 By equating Zionism with racism, the party has sparked a predictable wave of outrage. But are we debating the right questions? Green Party leader Zack Polanski speaks in London on 25 April 2026 (Justin Tallis/AFP) Off The fallout from the UK Green Party passing a motion declaring that Zionism is a form of racism has been predictable, with a chorus of condemnation across the political establishment. Responding to this necessitates engaging with two key and interlinked questions: why is it correct to define Zionism as a racist ideology and political movement, and how do we ensure this motion takes the movement forwards and not backwards? Let’s begin by dealing with the intense and predictable critiques of the motion, which largely fall into two camps. The dominant one centres on the claim that there is only one definition of Zionism: the right of the Jewish people to self-determination. The other critique is that it is wrong to define Zionism as racist, because there are many competing definitions of the term, some of which are definitively not racist. The first argues that Zionism, as a developed ideology and political movement, centred on the claim that Jews should be regarded as a people with a collective right to self-determination - one that should be recognised via the establishment of a state in Palestine . (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Those who define anti-Zionism as racism suggest that to oppose Zionism is to deny the Jewish people the right to self-determination - a denial supposedly based on racist foundations. The International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)’s definition of antisemitism cited one example of antisemitism as “denying the Jewish people their right to self-determination, e.g., by claiming that the existence of a State of Israel is a racist endeavor”. Questions over whether the Jewish people constitute a nation have always been debated within the Jewish community. But even if one concedes that most Jewish people conceived of themselves as a nation before 1948, that does not equate to a right to establish a state in Palestine. Violent dispossession Indeed, such a right did not exist unless it was recognised and accepted by the majority Arab population of Palestine at the time of the establishment of the state of Israel. The only way Zionists could enact their claim and establish a state was via the violent dispossession of the indigenous population. This was openly acknowledged by many Zionist leaders, including Ze’ev Jabotinsky , the godfather of Likud, who wrote in 1923: “Zionist colonisation must either stop, or else proceed regardless of the native population. Which means that it can proceed and develop only under the protection of a power that is independent of the native population - behind an iron wall, which the native population cannot breach.” None of this is to deny that Zionism emerged in large part as a response to centuries of persecution of Jewish people, and their desire to achieve liberation from that persecution. But one people’s right not to be persecuted does not grant them a right to dispossess another people. The Green motion has achieved its task in provoking a conversation about these essential questions. Now, we must shape this conversation more broadly, outside the movement's echo chambers This takes us to the second argument, which maintains that there are different versions of Zionism which do not support the violent dispossession of the Palestinian people. Yet while there could be strains of Zionism not rooted in conceptions of Jewish supremacist rights in Palestine, the Green Party’s motion addresses Zionism as it was realised as a political project across history, and as an ideology that justifies that outcome. The state of Israel was established on the foundations of wholesale murder, forced dispossession and ethnic cleansing . It has always practised a system of racist domination over all Palestinians across historic Palestine, along with those it drove into exile and denied the right of return . The motion deals with what Zionism has actually meant for Palestinians. This takes us to the question of the strategic value of the motion, which has attracted wholesale condemnation across the political establishment, and even internally within the Green Party itself, with most MPs rejecting it - all predictable developments, given the terrain we inhabit. Being strategic means having a clear theory of change, and an understanding of how a proposed course of action can increase the size and power of a movement, or conversely diminish it. For me, that theory of change has always rested on the belief that what is required to achieve the liberation of the Palestinian people is their ongoing resistance though all means they choose within the scope of international law , alongside external pressure placed on Israel to isolate it economiclly, politically, militarly and culturally. Building momentum In the UK context, this requires building a mass movement that can exert pressure to end all state complicity with Israel’s system of oppression. It is a strategy that has made huge gains over the past three years, in response to what people have come to see - and have been enabled to see - as a genocide . Building support for that movement has required a shift in the common public understanding of what has historically been defined as a territorial conflict, but is now recognised more widely as a framework of racist oppression backed by imperial powers. The question is therefore: how can this motion act to advance, and not diminish, that momentum? (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); In terms of the current dynamics of British politics, this matters hugely. We are seeing the Labour Party, worried by its loss of support , shifting its policy on Palestine, in significant but insufficient ways. A vibrant and united Green Party is a crucial factor in enabling continued pressure on Labour to move further. At the same time, the discourse around the motion has centred on how people define themselves, rather than on the realities of the racist oppression Palestinians face. Some within the movement are comfortable with that focus. A year ago, I was asked at a conference whether I agreed that the problem with Zionism was not its impact upon Palestinians, but its essential character as a racist ideology. In response, I paraphrased civil rights leader Kwame Ture (formerly Stokely Carmichael): “If a man wants to lynch me, that’s his problem. If he’s got the power to lynch me, that’s my problem.” This does not mean that we compromise on our understanding of Zionism and the realities of the oppression of Palestinians. It does mean that we avoid building roadblocks to people becoming part of the mass movement for change. Barriers to entry The problem we are confronting is not just a territorial conflict, but a situation where a state has institutionalised and legalised a system of racist domination. Being clear about that reality is crucial to ending complicity. This explains why actions such as those undertaken by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband , which focus only on the occupation , are inadequate. But the question about whether the best route to enabling this broader understanding is a discourse about the ideology of Zionism, and how it developed, is a strategic one. Are we more likely to persuade a public body to fully divest from all complicit companies if we insist that in doing so, they must also declare themselves to be anti-Zionist? What’s shameful is that no party before the Greens called Zionism racist Read More » Likewise, if our question to any prospective ally becomes “do you support a single democratic state”, then we are creating barriers to entry. Green leader Zack Polanski was right to say that he would have sought to amend that part of the motion, on the basis that this issue is for Palestinians - and not external parties - to determine. There is no single body that speaks for Palestinians, but the leadership of the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions ( BDS ) movement represents the biggest consensus across Palestinian civil society. They do not declare a position on a one-state or two-state solution , but rather express a clear consensus about the rights that must be realised to achieve liberation, within a framework of antiracism. That framework enables us to say that the realisation of Palestinian rights - to self-determination, return and equality - is not compatible with any solution that leaves intact an ethno-nationalist, Jewish supremacist state. Framing the conversation in this manner is crucial. In recent years, the Green Party has made great strides in its positioning, with motions recognising the realities of apartheid and genocide, and supporting BDS. The party must not succumb under pressure to retreat from these positions. The task is to shift the current terrain of debate. Decree 26‑310 introduces stricter conditions for the accreditation, operation and oversight of private schools. Its most significant provision is the prohibition of foreign curricula, including the French programme that had long been offered informally by several dozen establishments. Under the new rules, Arabic becomes mandatory as the language of instruction for all subjects, except foreign languages. Schools must use nationally approved textbooks and prepare pupils exclusively for Algerian state examinations. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The decree also stipulates that private institutions may not enter into any cooperation agreement with foreign bodies or schools without prior written authorisation from the education minister. Private schools have three years to comply, after which they face sanctions, including closure. This tightening of control over private education is part of a broader state strategy aimed at reasserting linguistic sovereignty and reducing the influence of French, widely seen as a legacy of the colonial period. France ruled Algeria from 1830 to 1962 and only left the country after a bloody war of independence that left up to a million people dead. Native Algerian Muslims were subject to discriminatory measures by the French administration, which settled the country with Europeans and ruled it as an extension of Metropolitan France. Since 2021, inspectors have carried out surprise visits to ensure that private schools were not prioritising the French curriculum, which some establishments had been teaching exclusively. In Algeria, new focus on English in schools rekindles debate over French colonial legacy Read More » In 2023, schools linked to the French Agency for French Education Abroad (AEFE) were ordered to withdraw from its labelling system, under threat of closure or legal action. The new decree also comes amid a major linguistic shift. Last month, three years after its introduction in primary education, English has become the first foreign language taught to pupils, starting from the third grade. The long‑running debate over the place of French in Algerian education has intensified in recent years, fuelled by diplomatic tensions between Algiers and Paris. Critics warn that the end of foreign programmes may leave many pupils struggling. Thousands of families relied on the French curriculum as a pathway to higher education in France. Teachers say some students, educated almost entirely in French, now find it difficult to follow the national syllabus. Others denounce rushed measures, arguing that the education system is not prepared and that these decisions stem more from political motives aimed at breaking with French influence than from a coherent educational strategy. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs390.23 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs396.96 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Oct 16 (Friday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

IHC seeks PTI response in case about Imran’s X account. ISLAMABAD: The Isla­mabad High Court (IHC) on Thursday granted PTI interim chairman Barris­ter Gohar Ali Khan additional time to submit a written response to a petition seeking a ban on party founder Imran Khan’s official X account, adjourning the hearing until Nov 23. Justice Arbab Muham­mad Tahir heard the petition, filed by Ghulam Mur­taza, while Barrister Gohar appeared in person. The court observed that Barrister Gohar could have submitted his response in writing. The PTI leader told the court his party did not cla­im ownership of the X ac­­c­ount in question. However, citing a change in circumstances, he sought additional time to submit a detailed response. Meanwhile, Judicial Magistrate Shaista Kundi issued arrest warrants for the accused who failed to appear in cases registered against the PTI founder and others in connection with the 2014 sit-in. Mr Khan could not be produced in court as he is currently incarcerated in Adiala jail. The magistrate then adjourned proceedings till Nov 25 and directed that evidence be presented at the next hearing. Published in Dawn, October 16th, 2026

Textile exports rise. ISLAMABAD: Pakis­tan’s textile and clothing exports rose 5.26 per cent to $5.026 billion in the first quarter of 2026-27 from $4.775bn in the same period last year. The marginal rise in export proceeds was attributed to elevated input costs, which eroded exporters’ competitiveness, and external shocks that disrupted shipments, according to data from the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics released on Thursday. Textile exporters have already warned the government that exports could slow further in the second quarter if no corrective measures are taken. Two major setbacks mainly contributed to slowing exports — suspension of trade with Afghanistan since October 2025 and falling exports to the Middle East due to the prevailing war in the region, especially the United Arab Emirates. PBS data showed readymade garment exports surged 15.69pc in value and 17.38pc in quantity during July-September FY27, while knitwear rose 4.14pc in value but fell 0.46pc in quantity. By contrast, bedwear dipped 0.07pc in value and 0.71pc in quantity. Pakistan’s oil import bill rose 6.50pc in 1QFY27 to $4.02bn from $3.77bn a year ago. Data showed import of crude oil jumped 23.10pc in value, with a decline of 6.87pc in quantity, indicating that the higher value of crude oil is due to rising international oil prices.
