Niger Wrestles with the Aftermath of a Military Revolt mloukili Thu, 10/08/2026 - 16:13 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Nigerien soldiers participating in a rally in support of General Abdourahamane Tiani (not seen) outside the former National Assembly in Niamey, on 2 September, 2026. AFP. Q&A / Africa 08 October 2026 11 minutes Niger Wrestles with the Aftermath of a Military Revolt A mutiny by Niger’s special forces in late August morphed into a coup attempt. In this Q&A, Crisis Group experts explain how the unrest exposed growing discontent within the military’s ranks. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Niger What is happening? Niger’s military leadership continues to reel from a coup attempt that exposed serious divides within the defence and security forces. On 28-29 August, soldiers from Niger’s Special Forces began shooting in their barracks at Air Base 101, which lies within the compound of Niamey’s international airport and houses most of the country’s military aircraft, as well as army units and foreign troops. Unrest quickly spread: groups of soldiers attacked the state broadcaster and the presidential palace, both in the city centre. Whether the incident began as a mutiny or whether it was meant from the start to oust General Abdourahamane Tiani, who seized power in a July 2023 coup, remains unclear. But the ramification of an uprising by a group of well-trained soldiers unhappy with their conditions of service and recent battlefield setbacks could be significant – particularly if it deepens divisions within the armed forces and disrupts their operations at a time when jihadist threats are looming large across several parts of the country. Members of the Special Reconnaissance Battalion for Special Operations Command, known by the French acronym BSR-COS, appear to have been behind the coup attempt, although a small number of soldiers from other units may have joined. Loyalist forces, particularly the presidential guard that Tiani commanded from 2011 to 2023, fought back as gunfire and detonations shook the capital, while national radio and television temporarily stopped broadcasting. By midday on 29 August, the mutineers withdrew to Air Base 101, where they unsuccessfully sought to rally other units to join them in toppling the government. Their stand did not last long, however. By the evening, national TV was up and running again, broadcasting images of loyalist forces arresting dozens, including at least one female soldier. A few days later, the government organised a national funeral for three members of the presidential guard forces who died in the clashes, while media reported that at least 27 mutineers were killed. The clashes further unsettled civilians in the capital, where heavy gunfire and explosions had already jolted residents twice this year, in January and June, when jihadists attacked the international airport, leaving many increasingly anxious about their safety. Why did the soldiers rebel? Tensions had been building within the BSR-COS for some time. In the days leading up to the revolt some soldiers had reportedly refused to go on a mission, citing a lack of adequate equipment. The battalion’s commander, Major Boubacar Maïhatchi, was detained soon after in the town of Tera as he returned from a mission escorting supply trucks from neighbouring Burkina Faso. Social media platforms have portrayed Maïhatchi as popular among younger officers, who respect his bravery and concern for his troops. His arrest may have prompted the soldiers’ decision to turn against the military leadership. The BSR-COS is part of Niger’s elite special forces, trained and equipped to work specifically in high-danger zones. As jihadist violence intensified in western Niger starting in the mid-2010s, the government expanded these forces, creating additional battalions, often with training and equipment from Western partners such as the U.S., France, and Germany. Today, there are more than a dozen battalions of roughly 500 to 600 soldiers each. The BSR-COS is among the most recently established units, with its members receiving training in Morocco. These battalions are leading the fight against jihadist insurgencies in Niger, including Islamic State Sahel Province and Jama’ at Nusratul Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) in the west. From its headquarters at Air Base 101, the BSR-COS has frequently assisted units under attack from jihadists or escorted convoys travelling through dangerous areas. In November 2025, for instance, Niger sent 82 fuel tankers to Mali to ease shortages caused by a JNIM blockade on the city. Members of the battalion led the military escort that protected the vehicles during the 1,400 km journey. While special forces battalions are valuable to the fight against jihadists, they are also capable of posing a serious threat to the military regime. Since winning independence from France in 1960, Niger has experienced five coups and several failed coup attempts. The army has long held sway in politics. Seven of its eleven presidents have been military officers. Given that history, Niger’s leaders are understandably wary of powerful military units. Where to deploy the special forces often presents the authorities with a dilemma. As the jihadist threat draws closer to the capital, their presence is increasingly indispensable to protect strategic localities and sites. At the same time, their proximity to the seat of power also fuels concerns within the military regime about the risk of yet another coup. The BSR-COS was initially expected to deploy to Ayorou, a jihadist hotspot near the Malian border where the government is building a large dam crucial for electricity and irrigation. That deployment was delayed in part because of militant attacks on Air Base 101 in January and again in June 2026. Why are soldiers unhappy with Niger’s top military leaders? The incident revealed a widening gap between the military leadership and the rank and file. The July 2023 coup brought senior officers from various components of the defence and security forces to power, ranging from the presidential guard and the army to the gendarmerie and the national guard. Together, these senior figures formed the National Council for Safeguarding the Homeland, which shapes government policy and military strategy. Four generals wielded the most influence in the council: Abdourahmane Tiani, who had himself sworn in for a five-year presidential term in 2025; Defence Minister Salifou Mody, his second-in-command; Mohamed Toumba, who heads the interior and security ministry; and armed forces chief of staff Moussa Salao Barmou, who has since been removed. Yet beneath the military brass that had seized control of the country, discontent has been simmering in the lower ranks. The senior officers justified their power grab partly by accusing the civilian government they toppled of failing to tackle the jihadist threat. Three years on, insecurity has grown and spread to more parts of the country; the opening of new fronts has stretched the defence and security forces thin. Troops are deployed to the front line more frequently and remain there longer. Foot soldiers complain that they lack adequate weapons and equipment. They allege air or ground reinforcements are slow to arrive when needed, if they arrive at all. Combat vehicles and pickup trucks are often in poor shape and the government has been slow to replace them, which makes working in high-risk zones hazardous. Conditions in military barracks have added to soldiers’ frustrations. Some have posted images on social media of the poor-quality meals they are served; others pool their money and buy condiments to improve their rations. On top of that, a recent wave of jihadist attacks – in Diffa, Dosso, Tillabery and Niamey – has killed dozens, draining troop morale. Senior command seems aware of the rumblings. The defence minister, the chief of army staff and other generals have made multiple visits to military bases to listen to soldiers’ concerns. They often blame sanctions imposed by foreign powers after the July 2023 coup for hampering their ability to procure arms. Most of these sanctions have since been lifted, however, and many soldiers appear unconvinced by the senior leadership’s explanation for the lack of equipment. In several instances soldiers’ frustration has manifested in defiance. The August revolt was Niger’s fourth episode of military unrest in less than two years. In June 2025, after an attack in Banibangou in northern Tillabery killed over 70 military personnel, soldiers assigned to retake the position protested and beat the officer in charge, who was later evacuated for medical treatment. A few days later, soldiers in the Zinder region mutinied and tried to kill their superior. In August 2025, soldiers in Ayorou rebelled and opened fire on their commander. As one officer puts it, “A mutiny is first and foremost a failure of leadership”. What did the coup attempt and its aftermath reveal about military divisions? The incident broke an unwritten rule that has long guided Niger’s military: namely, it is essential to avoid internal confrontations between different branches of the armed forces. In 2023, various military units opposed Tiani’s move to detain then-President Mohamed Bazoum in order to remove him from office, but senior commanders ultimately decided to avert an open conflict and rally behind Tiani’s power grab. This time around, the mutineers fought the presidential guard, while the government asked Russia’s Africa Corps to help quell the revolt. Hours after the August revolt had subsided, Russia’s ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropayev, told reporters that Russian forces had helped subdue the dissidents. Around 200 men from Africa Corps, the expeditionary force controlled by Russia’s defence ministry, have been deployed in Niger, including at Air Base 101, since 2024. They have assisted the regime with intelligence gathering, training on drone use, and operating air-defence systems. Russian forces reportedly used kamikaze drones that explode upon impact to force the mutineers to surrender. Some within the military found the involvement of foreigners in an internal confrontation particularly grating. Rumours have it that armed forces chief of staff Barmou may have been among those who voiced reservations about the Africa Corps’ intervention against the mutineers. In any event, on 11 September Tiani replaced Barmou with General Mamane Sani Kiaou, a move observers interpreted as aimed at reasserting control over the army. Barmou was also among the first generation of Nigerien special forces officers trained by the U.S. in the 2000s; he had reportedly threatened to resign previously over the army’s lack of equipment and his limited influence over military decision-making. Regime authorities, meanwhile, arrested over a hundred soldiers, while dozens of others, including special forces members, remain unaccounted for. Several civilians were also arrested, including two former ministers and a prominent journalist. The coup attempt could accentuate the resentment many troops feel vis-à-vis the presidential guard. The elite unit has long had access to the best equipment and the most talented recruits. It also foiled several coup attempts in the 2010s and early 2020s, leading some in the armed forces to perceive the guard as preoccupied with policing the military and protecting the regime rather than national security. Finally, the failed coup demonstrated that public support for the military regime is declining. The generals’ promises to restore security, overhaul governance, and assert Niger’s sovereignty on the international stage won a degree of sympathy from the public early on. But much of that enthusiasm has evaporated amid repeated security setbacks and an economic slowdown, partly attributable to the departure of Western donors and the closing of many NGOs by the government. On the afternoon of the coup attempt, regime supporters called on Niamey residents to turn out in support of the military leadership; notably, only a few dozen people did so. How did the incident reverberate in the region? The unrest had major diplomatic repercussions. The following day, a Nigerien officer speaking on national television alleged that he had received calls and messages from contacts in Chad, France, Belgium and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), informing him that several foreign countries – including Chad, Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and France – were prepared to intervene in support of those who had seized Air Base 101. He said they were operating with the blessing of the Economic Community of West Africa, the regional bloc from which Niger – alongside Burkina Faso and Mali – withdrew in 2025. On 3 September, the government spokesperson accused France of orchestrating the mutiny and alleged that “other African countries” had supported Paris. Some of these accusations were unsurprising. Tiani has repeatedly accused Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and France of conspiring against him, allegations the countries have rejected. But the regime’s claims that Chad was somehow also intent on destabilising Niger were new. Niger’s relations with Chad have soured in recent months. Niger’s authorities and their counterparts in Chad have traded accusations of tolerating, or even supporting, armed opposition groups active in their common border zones. Chadian officials did not respond to the allegations, although President Mahamat Idriss Déby later posted Quranic verse on social media warning against mixing truth with falsehoods. At the same time, the failed coup brought northern neighbour Algeria closer to the Nigerien authorities. Algeria condemned the incident and sent its chief of army staff to Niamey along with four fighter jets and a refuelling aircraft. The deployment of the fighter jets was apparently aimed at sending a strong message of support and to deter any attempt by foreign interests to dislodge the regime. The gesture also reinforced a diplomatic thaw already under way between the two countries. Relations had deteriorated last year after Algeria shot down a Malian drone near its border, prompting Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger – the three members of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) – to recall their ambassadors from Algiers. Niger and Algeria have since taken several steps toward rapprochement, culminating in President Tiani’s visit to Algiers in February. The episode has also reinforced Niger’s relationship with Russia. Moscow’s intervention demonstrated the growing importance of Russian security support to the authorities in Niamey. In turn, the episode could deepen the regime’s dependence on Moscow for its survival. Since the coup, most Western forces have left Niger, including U.S. and French troops, as well as German, Belgian and Canadian personnel involved in training the Nigerien armed forces. Today, only a few hundred Italian troops remain, making Italy the last Western country with a military presence in Niger. What should the authorities do next? The Nigerien authorities should exercise restraint during their ongoing post-coup crackdown. While those within the BSR-COS who instigated the mutiny will likely face sanctions, the authorities should spare the rank and file who simply followed commanders’ orders. Thus far, over a hundred soldiers have been arrested. A sweeping purge risks further weakening the armed forces, deepening mistrust between ranks and damaging troop morale at a time when Niger is under enormous pressure from jihadists and rebel groups. Restraint will not address the grievances that helped fuel the revolt, however. The authorities should tackle soldiers’ concerns about inadequate equipment, housing and food. A leaked 2020 defence audit exposed widespread corruption in procurement practices. In February 2024, however, Niger’s military authorities issued an ordinance exempting defence and security procurement from ordinary state contracting and public accounting oversight. Without compromising legitimate security concerns, the authorities could adopt a stronger approach to rooting out wrongdoing in the acquisition of military equipment, as well as improve living conditions in the barracks. The authorities should also tread carefully in order not to deepen divisions between different wings of the defence and security forces. Even symbolic decisions matter. The national funeral held for three presidential guard soldiers reinforced perceptions of double standards: regular soldiers who are killed in the line of duty are often buried quietly and rarely honoured publicly. A more equitable recognition of soldiers’ sacrifices could help reduce resentment across the ranks. More fundamentally, Niamey needs to reduce the mounting burden on its armed forces. The authorities should develop a comprehensive strategy for dealing with the proliferation of conflict fronts, giving greater weight to non-military approaches. Where possible, dialogue and diplomacy could help pacify restive areas. Even if such approaches do not produce sustainable peace, they could help demobilise combatants, achieve temporary ceasefires, and possibly reduce the number of simultaneous conflicts, providing relief to armed forces that show growing signs of fatigue. Finally, the authorities should recognise that military discontent is unfolding in an increasingly closed political environment. With political parties dissolved and civic space severely restricted, peaceful avenues for expressing dissatisfaction with the government have narrowed considerably. In such an environment, the armed forces risk becoming one of the few remaining channels through which opposition to the regime can erupt, and potentially in its most dangerous form. Reopening political and civic space would allow grievances to be expressed through less destabilising channels, even if doing so exposes the authorities to greater public criticism. On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 10/09/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 09 October 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 9 October 2026 HAITI Haiti’s electoral council announced changes to the country’s voting rules Tuesday. The new law, which will likely result in delays to polls presently scheduled for 13 December, will remove provisions that would have disqualified individuals subject to bilateral sanctions imposed by third countries from running for office. Those subject to UN sanctions remain barred from candidacy. The move comes as the UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, which makes private recommendations to the Security Council regarding who should be sanctioned, denounced several high-profile politicians for using gangs to fuel violence. Some UN Security Council members worry that sanctioning public figures could interfere with Haiti’s political process. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the risk of inaction is greater, however: those who have collaborated with gangs could return to power, further delaying resolution of the Haitian conflict. MALI On Tuesday, the Malian army recaptured Kidal, a strategically important city in the country’s north that had been held by the separatist Front for the Liberation of Azawad (FLA) since April. The FLA said it had decided to temporarily withdraw from Kidal as the army, backed by Russian Africa Corps paramilitaries, launched a large-scale offensive. Crisis Group expert Ibrahim Maïga says the recapture of Kidal is a significant military development. But without a political process to build on these gains, the takeover alone is unlikely to bring this conflict closer to a lasting resolution. UKRAINE A Russian attack on Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region killed at least 33 people on a public bus Thursday. Previous Russian strikes across the country Wednesday killed at least 28 others, including 22 when a missile hit a residential building. Kramatorsk – one of the cities Russia has been unable to capture in Donetsk – has become an important supply hub for the Ukrainian army. The attack came as Kyiv struck a data centre belonging to Russia’s largest technology company, Yandex, in the central Ryazan region, south east of Moscow. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says both sides are using long-range strikes to put pressure on their adversaries, though Russia’s aerial campaign is far more devastating, raising the number of casualties among the civilian population and upending daily life for millions. 2 October 2026 MYANMAR Military airstrikes on a market in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, on Monday reportedly killed at least 50 people. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these tit-for-tat attacks on hydrocarbon infrastructure signal a new phase in the conflict, now entering its fourth week, as a global energy crisis looms and Gulf Arab states are increasingly caught in the crossfire, with Saudi Arabia warning of military action against Iran as these states’ patience wears thin. NIGERIA Multiple suicide bombings Monday killed at least 26 people and injured over a hundred in Maiduguri, capital of Nigeria’s Borno state. The attacks mark the second deadliest incident in Maiduguri in the past five years. No group has yet claimed responsibility. The bombings come amid a surge of violence in the country’s north east, with both Boko Haram and the Islamic State-West Africa Province, an ISIS affiliate, launching lethal raids. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says the latest attacks indicate that these insurgencies may again be gaining momentum. The Nigerian government and its foreign partners should step up efforts to counter the new challenge and halt rising insecurity in other parts of the country. 13 March 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Drone strikes killed several people Tuesday night in Goma, capital of North Kivu province in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, including a French woman working with UNICEF and at least two other residents. The M23 rebels who hold the city blamed the Congolese government for the attacks. Kinshasa said an investigation is under way. Despite a formal ceasefire in their conflict, both the Congolese government and the M23 (backed by Rwandan troops) have been acquiring drones as a means of getting around enemy defences. Tuesday’s attacks, along with another in February that killed M23 spokesperson Willy Ngoma, mark a dramatic escalation in the conflict’s aerial warfare. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says Kinshasa, which has purchased Chinese and Turkish drones, is determined to use its new arsenal to show the rebels they are not safe in their bastions. But with civilian casualties mounting, the government’s growing reliance on drones could backfire by costing it international support. Having flexed its muscles, Kinshasa would be well advised to return to the diplomatic arena, pressing for Rwandan withdrawal from the country and returning to negotiations with the M23 with a stronger hand. IRAN Amid a widening Middle East conflict sparked by U.S.-Israeli strikes that began two weeks ago, the Islamic Republic effected only the second transition in its most senior post since the 1979 revolution that brought it to power. Mojtaba Khamenei has taken up the position of Supreme Leader, which his father Ali held from 1989 until his death on 28 February in the war’s opening salvo. The U.S.-Israeli campaign has continued unabated, doing significant damage. Iran has responded with drone and missile strikes in the Gulf and brought traffic in the Strait of Hormuz to a crawl. The first official statement attributed to the younger Khamenei was defiant in tone, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, highlighting the Iranian regime's desire to project continuity under duress, vis-à-vis both its foreign adversaries and its domestic opponents. But that ambition could be short-lived if Khamenei is targeted amid the hostilities or outmanoeuvred by other players in the regime's upper echelons. Many Iranians, meanwhile, are despairing at a leadership transition that so far promises more of the same. LEBANON Israel’s latest military escalation in Lebanon continued to wreak havoc this week. Since 2 March, when Hizbollah fired rockets toward Israeli territory for the first time in over a year, Israel has ramped up aerial bombardment, including of the capital Beirut, and forced hundreds of thousands to flee their homes. It has also sent more troops into southern Lebanon, with a view to establishing what it calls a “security zone” there. While Israel retains military superiority over Hizbollah, the Shiite party-cum-militia has put up a fight. On Wednesday, it launched a barrage of 100 rockets across the border, which triggered an especially brutal sequence of Israeli air raids. Crisis Group expert David Wood says neither of the belligerents appears ready to stop, even as Lebanese leaders scramble to find a diplomatic off-ramp. Already, the Lebanese public has paid a horrific price: the death toll has climbed to almost 700, and thousands more have seen their homes and communities destroyed. 6 March 2026 IRAN The U.S. and Israel launched massive airstrikes on Iran Saturday, hitting military installations and killing senior leaders, including Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. In retaliation, Iran fired missiles and drones at Israel, as well as U.S. bases and commercial infrastructure in Gulf states. The conflict's reverberations have quickly spread from the Indian Ocean to the eastern Mediterranean. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Tehran looks prepared for a drawn-out confrontation, betting that it can steadily raise the psychological and economic costs to its adversaries, while maintaining cohesion at the top of the political system despite Khamenei’s demise. The U.S.-Israeli campaign appears open-ended, with no clear objective yet defined. Airstrikes can substantially degrade Iran's military capabilities but are unlikely to dislodge the regime, and even if they did, state collapse in Iran would risk unleashing far wider regional disorder. AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Border clashes continued this week after Pakistan declared “open war” with Afghanistan last Friday. The declaration followed Taliban retaliatory cross-border attacks after Pakistani airstrikes on purported Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) targets in Afghanistan on 21 February. Pakistan then carried out another series of strikes on 27 February, including in Kabul. Islamabad accuses Taliban authorities of sheltering the TTP, which has stepped up attacks in Pakistan. Kabul denies it. According to the UN, the latest fighting has killed dozens of civilians in Afghanistan and displaced tens of thousands, with reports also indicating civilian casualties in Pakistan. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says a drawn-out conflict serves neither side's interests. Outside actors should press Islamabad and Kabul to de-escalate. ECUADOR The U.S. Southern Command said Tuesday Ecuadorian and U.S. forces had begun operations to curb organised crime in Ecuador. They first went after the Colombian armed group Comandos de la Frontera, which is active along the Colombian border. Ecuador’s military says the operations will continue indefinitely. While details are classified, news reports indicate that the U.S. played an advisory role, without putting troops on the ground. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says such cooperation is not new, but the latest announcement signals deeper U.S. involvement. Security ties have deepened as President Daniel Noboa aligns with the Trump administration’s preference for using military force to combat drug trafficking. 27 February 2026 CHAD - SUDAN Chadian authorities Monday announced the immediate closure of the country’s border with Sudan. The decision followed what N’Djamena described as “repeated incursions” linked to Sudan’s war, after clashes around the Sudanese border town of Tina involving the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and militias aligned with Sudan’s army. Chad said the border would remain closed until further notice, while allowing humanitarian exemptions, including for refugees and returnees, as well as approved aid deliveries. Crisis Group expert Charles Bouëssel says N’Djamena should maintain vital cross-border aid and preserve trade that sustains displaced populations. It should also ensure that security and disarmament operations in the east are conducted with restraint and impartiality to contain intercommunal tensions and prevent Chad from being drawn further into Sudan’s war. CUBA Cuban authorities Wednesday accused ten people on a U.S.-registered speedboat carrying weapons and tactical gear of attempting infiltration of Cuban territory with “terrorist intentions”. Border guards shot four people dead and wounded six others aboard the boat after its occupants allegedly opened fire. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any U.S. involvement and said Washington would investigate the facts independently. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the incident comes amid already high tensions between Havana and Washington, after the U.S. halted fuel imports coming into Cuba, exacerbating a severe energy crisis on the island, in hopes of pushing the Cuban authorities to negotiate an economic and political opening. SYRIA ISIS released an audio statement last weekend denouncing Syria’s interim government and calling for a renewed campaign against its forces. The jihadist group has since claimed responsibility for several attacks on Syrian army personnel in the northern and north-eastern parts of the country. These developments follow last month’s reported mass escape from the al-Hol camp, which held over 20,000 detainees, many of them relatives of suspected ISIS fighters. Some of these people got away as security broke down during an offensive led by Damascus on the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the closure of the camp compounds an already risky convergence. With the SDF sidelined, U.S. forces withdrawing from Syria and the new government’s security apparatus still finding its feet, ISIS seems to be seeking an opening to resume its insurgency. 20 February 2026 MATERNAL MORTALITY The World Health Organization released a study Tuesday showing that nearly two thirds of maternal deaths worldwide occur in countries wracked by conflict or instability. Crisis raises the risks associated with pregnancy, the report finds, though health services in conflict-affected places are generally already scarce. Some countries, such as Colombia and Ethiopia, have made progress in reducing maternal mortality through partnerships with NGOs with expertise in service provision in remote areas. But now aid cuts have put such programs in jeopardy, says Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing, even as women are dying in childbirth at alarming rates. Donor funds still available should be directed toward bolstering community-based health services, particularly in war zones, through such cost-effective means as midwifery. NIGERIA The Nigerian government announced Tuesday that the U.S. will dispatch 100 additional military personnel to assist in fighting jihadist groups in the northern part of the country. This deployment comes amid deadly attacks that killed 56 people in Niger state last weekend and 34 others in Kebbi state on Wednesday. These raids are part of a broader surge of violence that has claimed over 250 lives across north-central and north-western Nigeria in the past month. Hundreds more people have been abducted. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says jihadists and other armed groups are growing stronger in these regions and elsewhere, by exploiting gaps in rural and border security as government forces become increasingly overstretched. The U.S. aid notwithstanding, the government needs to urgently improve its response, including by expediting measures outlined under the “nationwide security emergency” President Bola Tinubu declared last November. U.S. - IRAN Iranian and U.S. delegations convened in Geneva Tuesday for talks about Tehran’s nuclear program, the second round of such negotiations this month. In parallel, the Islamic Republic’s foreign minister met with the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency for technical discussions. Both Iran and the U.S. noted a measure of progress, as did the Omani mediators, even as Washington continues to ramp up its deployment of military assets to the Middle East. But the gaps between the sides are still wide, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, even as regards what a possible agreement would cover. The negotiators have yet to wrestle with matters of substance. Tehran and Washington are aware of the high risks of failure, as well as the costs that fresh hostilities would bring. Yet the pace of diplomacy is lagging as momentum builds for confrontation. 13 February 2026 BANGLADESH The Bangladesh Nationalist Party won a landslide victory Thursday in the country’s first national elections since the 2024 ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, whose Awami League was barred from contesting the vote. A concurrent referendum on the July Charter – a set of reforms negotiated by all the participating parties over the last year – passed by a wide margin. Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean says the turnout and referendum result reflect the credibility of both the election and the reform process in the eyes of most Bangladeshis. The incoming government will face daunting challenges, however, such as getting Bangladesh’s ailing economy back on track and improving security. ERITREA-ETHIOPIA Addis Ababa accused Eritrea of deploying its troops into Ethiopian territory Saturday to conduct joint manoeuvres with Ethiopian rebels along the border. In response, Asmara said Ethiopia had fabricated evidence for this charge, asserting that it has “no appetite for or desire to engage in meaningless acrimony”. Crisis Group expert Magnus Taylor says this latest confrontation comes shortly after renewed clashes between Ethiopia and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front’s armed wing, which Addis Ababa alleges has formed a secret pact with Eritrea. More fighting could be in the offing if efforts to de-escalate tensions fail. WEST BANK Israel’s security cabinet Sunday approved measures that further cement Israeli control of the occupied West Bank, with the explicit goal of pre-empting the establishment of a viable Palestinian state. The move reflects an Israeli plan not only to annex all the Israeli settlements in the rural West Bank, but also to further limit what is left of nominal Palestinian autonomy and displace Palestinians from more built-up areas. Absent action that conditions trade and aid to Israel on policy changes, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein, international support for a two-state solution increasingly rings hollow. The annexation drive also undermines the Trump administration’s twenty-point plan for Gaza. 6 February 2026 GAZA Israel carried out strikes across the Gaza Strip Wednesday, killing at least 24 Palestinians. The Israeli army claimed it was targeting a Hamas commander and responding to fire upon its troops, but civilians accounted for most of the casualties. The death toll among Palestinians in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire has now topped 550. Humanitarian needs also remain acute amid aid shortfalls; the Rafah crossing with Egypt has opened, after a long wait, but deliveries are still tightly restricted. Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein says the latest violence underscores how tenuous the ceasefire remains despite formally entering its second phase, when the sides are supposed to begin addressing issues of long-term security, governance and reconstruction. Diplomats need to press Israel to release its chokehold on Gaza and push for continued progress on the truce’s terms. PAKISTAN Police backed by soldiers reportedly killed more than 200 Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) fighters in raids throughout Balochistan, a south-western province next to Afghanistan, over the course of this week. The operations followed a rash of BLA attacks on police stations, military installations and residential areas that claimed 50 lives (33 civilians and 17 state personnel) over the weekend. Islamabad accuses the Afghan Taliban of harbouring the BLA high command, which they also say gets financial and logistical assistance from Pakistan’s arch-rival India. Crisis Group Executive Vice President Richard Atwood says the high death toll among the Baloch separatist insurgents shows that authorities planned the raids carefully, with a view to keeping civilians out of the crossfire. But these events are bound to increase tensions between Islamabad and Kabul, which are already high following clashes between Pakistani and Afghan Taliban forces last October, and to further chill relations between Islamabad and New Delhi. U.S. - COLOMBIA Presidents Donald Trump and Gustavo Petro met at the White House Tuesday after months of heated rhetoric prompted by disputes over issues such as migration, counter-narcotics cooperation and the 3 January U.S. raid grabbing Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Amid these exchanges, Trump went so far as to suggest that Colombia, too, might be a target of U.S. military action. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting proved constructive, helping ease the tensions in the bilateral relationship and signalling that the two countries can continue working together to curb drug trafficking. The two presidents also discussed the tariff spat between Colombia and Ecuador, with Trump offering to mediate between these countries’ leaders. Resolving the immediate trade crisis could pave the way for stronger collaboration between Bogotá and Quito in fighting organised crime. 30 January 2026 COLOMBIA - ECUADOR The foreign ministers of Colombia and Ecuador met in Panama after a week in which a trade dispute escalated between the two countries. The standoff began last week, when Ecuador announced a 30 per cent tariff on Colombian imports, blaming Bogotá for insufficient action to stop drug trafficking along the shared border. Colombia retaliated with tariffs on Ecuadorian goods and a suspension of electricity exports. Ecuador then raised the fee for Colombian oil shipped through its pipelines tenfold from about $3 to $30 per barrel. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting indicates that the two capitals understand the dispute will hurt both economies as well as weaken both states’ ability to confront security challenges on the frontier. Rather than acting in isolation, the two should mount a coordinated cross-border response, which is likely to be more effective in fighting transnational criminal networks. IRAN U.S. President Donald Trump told Iran Wednesday that it risks "major destruction" if it fails to negotiate a nuclear deal with Washington. The ultimatum follows earlier warnings of U.S. intervention over the Islamic Republic's repression of protests. The U.S. has dispatched additional naval assets, airpower and defensive systems to the Middle East. Tehran – along with some of its non-state allies in the region – has threatened retaliation if attacked. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Iran is unlikely to meet the White House's sweeping demands, which encompass nuclear, missile and regional concessions, raising the likelihood of confrontation at a time when the Islamic Republic already faces increasing diplomatic isolation, mounting economic problems and outrage at its brutal crackdown on dissent. SOUTH SUDAN The South Sudanese army announced Sunday it is launching a major offensive to recapture territory in Jonglei state that has been seized by opposition forces and allied militias since hostilities intensified in December. The UN warned this week that mass troop mobilisation and inflammatory rhetoric from senior commanders have significantly heightened the risk of violence against civilians. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the escalation signals a clear slide toward full-scale war. The rapidly expanding conflict threatens to draw in neighbouring states, including Uganda, and to deepen South Sudan’s dangerous entanglement in the war in Sudan. 23 January 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO M23 rebels withdrew from Uvira, near the Burundian border, over last weekend, ending a tense month in which they controlled the South Kivu town. Of particular concern, says Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff, is the mounting ethnic tension in the area. The M23 insurgents, who portray themselves as defenders of the Tutsi people, took Uvira claiming that the Tutsi-related Banyamulenge living in town needed their protection. GUATEMALA President Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of emergency Monday after inmates had taken more than 45 guards hostage at three prisons two days earlier. After the authorities regained control of one of the facilities, gang members outside jail killed ten policemen in retaliation. The state of emergency limits citizens' rights and gives state forces special powers such as making arrests without cause. It echoes the iron-fist approaches to public safety pursued by leaders in El Salvador and Ecuador. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Arévalo, who won the 2024 election touting a progressive reform agenda but has since lost popularity, listened to demands from Guatemalans for a decisive response to an uptick in violent crime. The leading opposition candidate, Robert Kyagulanyi of the National Unity Party (NUP), rejected the result, alleging widespread fraud. He remains in hiding after dodging a police raid – staged for reasons that remain unclear – on his residence. AFP / Anthony Wallace Report 359 / Asia-Pacific 09 October 2026 20+ minutes Toward a Thaw in the Cambodia-Thailand Border Conflict Hostilities between Cambodia and Thailand ceased in late 2025, after two rounds of combat along the frontier. But the truce is under growing strain. To avoid more war, the two countries should restore normal diplomatic ties and resume work on demarcating their shared border. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print "> Download PDF Related Tags Thailand Cambodia What’s new? Fighting between Cambodia and Thailand over a border dispute killed at least 150 people and displaced almost a million more in 2025. Now, the ceasefire between the two countries is fraying, while diplomacy has stalled. Why does it matter? The 2025 combat was the costliest yet between the two countries and the worst confrontation ever between two members of the Association of South East Asian Nations. War could break out again if Bangkok and Phnom Penh do not improve relations. What should be done? Leaders in Bangkok and Phnom Penh should work to normalise diplomatic ties, reconvene the Joint Boundary Commission in order to resume the surveys that will let the sides demarcate the land border, when circumstances allow, and cooperate on a program of demining affected areas. Executive Summary After two rounds of fighting in 2025 over a longstanding territorial dispute along their 800km land border, a ceasefire between Cambodia and Thailand is under strain, threatened by heightened nationalism on both sides and mutual allegations of violations. Tensions between the two countries resurfaced early in 2025, erupting into combat that dwarfed earlier clashes in scale. When the shooting stopped on 27 December, Thailand had the upper hand, holding most of the contested areas as well as slivers of Cambodian territory. In May, Bangkok withdrew from a 2001 bilateral agreement on how to resolve overlapping maritime claims, leading Phnom Penh to initiate compulsory conciliation – a non-binding international legal proceeding – under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. In turn, Thailand suspended participation in bilateral mechanisms on land border demarcation, leaving negotiations in limbo. To avoid more war, the two countries should put nationalist fervour to the side and overcome their mistrust, starting with restoring normal diplomatic ties and resuming efforts to jointly demarcate the land border. Following an exchange of fire in May 2025 that killed a Cambodian soldier, fighting broke out along the border in late July. With Malaysian mediation, backed up by U.S. President Donald Trump’s vow to suspend trade talks with both countries so long as hostilities continued, the two sides agreed to a ceasefire after five days of combat. Tensions simmered over the following months, however, with regular confrontations between troops and a series of landmine explosions that wounded sixteen Thai soldiers. The ceasefire collapsed in November, and a second round of hostilities ensued, displacing almost a million people on both sides before halting with another truce, brokered this time with China’s help near year’s end. The conflict is linked to domestic politics in both countries. Border tensions were pivotal in the disqualification from office of Thailand’s Prime Minister Paetongtarn Shinawatra in 2025. Her successor Anutin Charnvirakul, leader of the Bhumjaithai (Thai Pride) Party, took office that September, dissolved parliament in December and won in a general election the next February, in part by maintaining a hard line on Cambodia amid a wave of Thai nationalism. The episode evoked memories of the 2008 conflict between Cambodia and Thailand, when royalist opponents of Paetongtarn’s father, the controversial former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, fanned nationalist discontent over the border to undermine the Thaksin-aligned government of the day. Nationalist zeal has also appeared to bolster the government of Prime Minister Hun Manet in Cambodia, though further fighting could shake the unity of the ruling Cambodian People’s Party and the regime built by his father, and current senate president, Hun Sen. While the ceasefire has held thus far, the conflict continues through diplomatic channels, with Cambodia decrying Thai occupation of its territory. While the ceasefire has held thus far, the conflict continues through diplomatic channels, with Cambodia decrying Thai occupation of its territory. Thailand insists it is observing the ceasefire agreement, which provides for troops to remain in positions they held when it came into effect, and accuses Cambodia of attempting to internationalise the dispute. Compulsory conciliation on the overlapping maritime claims will take at least a year to conclude. In the meantime, Bangkok has declined to resume the technical work of a Joint Boundary Commission to survey and demarcate the land border between the countries, while cooperation on demining the frontier has been suspended since the 2025 fighting. Both sides are angry, with each portraying the other as the obstacle to resolving the conflict. Amid the mutual recriminations, it would be easy for a minor border incident to blow up into something bigger, including a third bout of major fighting. Ideally, a third party would mediate between Cambodia and Thailand to head off the possibility of escalation. But several factors impede movement toward dialogue. First, strident nationalism on both sides makes compromise appear hazardous. In Bangkok, the government seems content with the status quo and is following the military’s lead on border security. In Phnom Penh, senior leaders recognise the risks another round of fighting could pose to the government’s legitimacy, but they cannot appear to be bending on sovereignty or territorial integrity. Confrontation continues, for now, to bring political rewards to decision-makers on both sides, especially the Thai military, which has been able to polish a tarnished image. Secondly, while the conflict has been economically damaging to both countries, it has not been sufficiently costly to precipitate a thaw in the interest of resuming cross-border commerce. Both Thai and Cambodian leaders perceive the political costs of conciliatory moves as greater than the prospective benefits. Thirdly, international powers have limited leverage to push the two sides toward a deal. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, the rotating chair of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 2025, took the lead in brokering the July ceasefire – with decisive help from Trump’s trade talks threat. But since that truce unravelled, the bloc has been unable to expedite resolution of the dispute. Current ASEAN chair the Philippines has used its good offices to bring the Cambodian and Thai prime ministers together, but it is in no position to spur dialogue. Preoccupied with the Middle East, the U.S. shows no interest in mediating. China would be able to convene talks, but it is unlikely to jeopardise its relations with either country by attempting to impose an agreement. Under these circumstances, immediate prospects for concerted efforts to resolve the border issue are poor. But until the dispute is resolved, the possibility of another war, with all the associated death, displacement and other human suffering, will remain. Both sides should dial down official rhetoric that casts the other as an enemy and seek areas of common interest, starting by normalising diplomatic relations and reposting ambassadors in the other’s capital. Though the Joint Boundary Commission has neither the mandate nor a mechanism to resolve the political impasse, its work of surveying and demarcating the border is a prerequisite for settling the dispute and should be restarted as soon as possible. Demining is a priority for both countries that should offer another politically acceptable platform for cooperation. Crucially, both border demarcation and demining are already stipulated in the ceasefire agreement. The alternative to honouring these truce terms that the two neighbours have agreed upon could be more bloodshed, which is highly unlikely to put this long-running border dispute to rest. Bangkok/Phnom Penh/Brussels, 9 October 2026 I. Introduction The border dispute between Cambodia and Thailand is hardly new, but the fighting that erupted between the two South East Asian neighbours in July and December 2025 was deadlier and more widespread than earlier clashes, killing at least 150 people and displacing roughly one million. 1 For background, see Crisis Group Asia Report N°215, Waging Peace: ASEAN and the Thai-Cambodian Border Conflict , 6 December 2011; and Matthew Wheeler, “ Border Dispute with Cambodia Sparks Political Disarray in Thailand ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 1 July 2025. See also “Situation Report 20 – Displacement Crisis as a Result of the Cambodia-Thailand Border Conflict”, World Vision International in Cambodia, 2 January 2026; and “Thai deadly border clashes displace over half a million in Cambodia”, France 24, 21 December 2025. By 27 December, when the parties reached the latest ceasefire, Thai troops had taken high ground in many locations along the 800km border, occupying contested areas as well as patches of Cambodian territory. 2 Given that portions of the border are undemarcated and disputed, its exact length is not known. Cambodia’s estimate is 817km; Thailand’s is 798km. Since then, the ceasefire has been tested regularly. Bangkok and Phnom Penh have made little progress toward delimiting the border or resuming normal diplomatic relations. The risk of a third round of war is real. In the wake of the 2025 fighting, bilateral relations are at a low ebb. Each side accuses the other of having started the conflict, while indulging in provocative rhetoric and actions that undermine prospects for resolution. Cambodia alleges that Thailand aims to annex parts of its territory seized in the December 2025 fighting. Thailand maintains that it is observing the ceasefire deal, which stipulates that troops remain in positions they held when the agreement entered into force. The territorial dispute extends out to sea as well. In May, Bangkok withdrew from a 2001 memorandum of understanding on overlapping maritime claims, leading Phnom Penh to initiate compulsory conciliation, a non-binding dispute resolution mechanism under the UN Convention of the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). This report examines the roots of the conflict, its domestic political drivers and the current diplomatic impasse. It is based on research conducted since February in Bangkok and Phnom Penh, including interviews with officials of both governments, some of whom have retired but have direct knowledge of developments, as well as diplomats, analysts and journalists covering the conflict. Women made up about a fifth of the interlocutors. Research was also carried out in Siem Reap and Anlong Veng in Cambodia, as well as in the Thai border provinces of Buriram, Sa Kaeo, Si Sa Ket and Surin. The report uses both Khmer and Thai place names on first reference. It uses the Khmer name for the 11th century Preah Vihear temple, known in Thai as Khao Phra Viharn, in view of the 1962 International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruling that the temple is situated in Cambodian territory. 3 “Case concerning the Temple of Preah Vihear (Cambodia v. Thailand)”, International Court of Justice (ICJ), 15 June 1962. After two rounds of fighting in 2025 over a longstanding territorial dispute along the 800km land border, a ceasefire between Cambodia and Thailand is under strain, threatened by heightened nationalism on both sides. The Weight of History The contemporary border conflict is a legacy of both colonialism and nationalist historical narratives, which elites in both Cambodia and Thailand have repeatedly exploited for domestic political advantage. A. Preah Vihear and Thailand’s “Lost Territories” In the 18th and 19th centuries, Siam and Vietnam vied for control of Cambodia, while Khmer kings sought room for manoeuvre by playing the larger powers against each other. 4 The Khmer Empire, renowned for building Angkor Wat, dominated mainland South East Asia from roughly the 9th to the 15th century. Siam gained suzerainty over what is now western Cambodia in 1794, but it did not actively colonise the area. 5 David Chandler, A History of Cambodia (Boulder, Colo., 2008), pp. 142-143; 183-184. France then established a protectorate over Cambodia in 1863, stopping the kingdom’s neighbours from swallowing it whole. In 1893, French gunboats dropped anchor in waters near the royal palace in Bangkok to press Siam to cede territories east of the Mekong River, as well as the eastern provinces of Chantaburi and Trat, to France. This event, known as the Pak Nam Crisis, marks the origin of a still-ubiquitous Thai historical narrative of “lost territories” sacrificed by King Chulalongkorn to preserve his domain from the encroachment of Western colonialism. 6 Thongchai Winichakul, Siam Mapped: A History of the Geo-Body 0f a Nation (Honolulu, Hawaii, 1994), pp. 111, 150-153; Shane Strate, The Lost Territories: Thailand’s History of National Humiliation (Honolulu, Hawaii, 2015). Franco-Siamese treaties of 1904 and 1907 established that the border between Siam and French Indochina would follow the watershed of the Dangrek Mountains. In 1908, Siam received a series of maps, drafted by a French expedition, depicting a border line. 7 The expedition that drafted the map was supposed to be a joint Franco-Siamese endeavour, but Siam did not send surveyors to participate. These maps, known as Annex I of the 1907 treaty, deviate from the treaty’s text; the border line departs from the watershed to place the ancient temple complex of Preah Vihear – a vestige of the Khmer empire – within French Indochina. Siamese officials did not detect the discrepancy until they made their own survey in 1934, but they raised no objection until much later. 8 Strate, The Lost Territories , op. cit., pp. 161-162. The 1:200,000-scale Annex I border maps remain the only legally recognised ones. In Thailand, Preah Vihear became a national cause under Field Marshal Phibun Songkhram, a strongman who governed the country from 1938 to 1944 and again from 1948 to 1957. In 1939, the Department of Education included the temple complex on maps of Thailand’s historical sites. During World War II, Thailand reclaimed Cambodia’s western provinces, encompassing the Preah Vihear complex. The Thai government promoted the temple as a symbol of territories earlier surrendered to colonial powers to retain Siam’s independence. 9 Ibid., pp. 162-163. As a condition for admission to the UN, Thailand then ceded the Cambodian provinces to France under the 1946 Washington Treaty, but it asserted Thai sovereignty over Preah Vihear after Cambodia gained independence in 1953. 10 Sok Udom Deth, A History of Cambodia-Thailand Diplomatic Relations, 1950-2020 (Glienicke, 2020), p. 26. In Thailand, press coverage of the [1958] negotiations stirred up nationalist sentiments, helping turn Preah Vihear [temple] into a popular issue. After years of wrangling, formal bilateral talks about the disputed temple began in 1958. In Thailand, press coverage of the negotiations stirred up nationalist sentiments, helping turn Preah Vihear into a popular issue. Similarly, Cambodia’s King Norodom Sihanouk promoted the historical monument as a national cause, portraying Thailand as a perennial threat to the nation’s sovereignty. 11 Strate, The Lost Territories , op. cit., pp. 165-166. Cambodia withdrew from negotiations in October 1959 and appealed to the ICJ to settle the dispute. In 1962, the court ruled that Preah Vihear was situated in Cambodian territory, reasoning that Siam’s failure to object to the Annex I map in the decades after it was issued signified acceptance. 12 “Case concerning the Temple of Preah Vihear (Cambodia v. Thailand)”, op. cit. In Thailand, the verdict inflamed popular opinion, helping entrench the idea of “lost territories” and national humiliation at the hands of Cambodia and colonial powers. 13 Strate, The Lost Territories , op. cit., p. 170. Satellite imagery of the Preah Vihear temple. Source: Google Earth / CRISIS GROUP B. Managing a Disputed Border The Khmer Rouge victory in Cambodia in 1975 opened a new chapter along the border. After Vietnam’s 1978 invasion of Cambodia, almost a million refugees fled to Thailand. Refugee camps became strongholds of armed groups, including the Khmer Rouge, resisting Vietnam’s occupation with Thai, Chinese and U.S. assistance. 14 Nicole Jenne, “The Thai-Cambodian Border Dispute: An Agency-centred Perspective on the Management of Interstate Conflict”, Contemporary Southeast Asia , vol. 29, n0. 2 (2017), p. 329. In the late 1980s, Thailand reoriented its regional diplomacy, seeking a change from “from battlefield to marketplace”. 15 Chatchai Choonhavan, Thai prime minister from 1988 to 1991, advanced this policy. Meanwhile, the 1991 Paris Peace Accords and the UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia brought relative peace and the prospect of economic development. In accordance with these changes, the two countries took steps to establish a new relationship, leading them to sign a bilateral agreement on border management in 1995. 16 “Agreement between the Government of the Kingdom of Thailand and the Government of the Kingdom of Cambodia on the Establishment of Border Committees”, Phnom Penh, 26 September 1995. This pact set up the General Border Committee (GBC), chaired by the countries’ defence ministers, and three Regional Border Committees (RBC), chaired by regional military commanders charged to “consider and agree on appropriate measures to promote cooperation in the maintenance of peace, order and stability in the border area”. 17 Ibid. The agreement empowered the RBCs to “solve specific problems that may arise” and promote cooperation and communication links “to enable immediate contact at all times”. 18 Ibid. The relevant commands are: Thailand’s 2nd Army Region and Cambodia’s 4th Military Region; Thailand’s 1st Army Region and Cambodia’s 5th Military Region; Thailand’s Chanthaburi-Trat Border Defence Command and Cambodia’s 3rd Military Region. The [Joint Boundary Commission] has ... succeeded in delimiting some 600km of the [Thailand-Cambodia] border, with roughly 200km outstanding. Five years later, Cambodia and Thailand signed a memorandum of understanding establishing a Joint Boundary Commission (JBC) to govern border surveys and demarcation. 19 “Memorandum of Understanding between the Government of the Kingdom of Thailand and the Government of the Kingdom of Cambodia on the Survey and Demarcation of Land Boundary”, 14 June 2000. This document – known as MOU 43 for the Buddhist year 2543 in which it was signed – provides for a five-step process, including identifying the 73 boundary markers installed between 1909 and 1919, jointly surveying the boundary and demarcating the border. In 2003, the two sides then agreed on Terms of Reference dividing the border into seven sectors. 20 “Terms of Reference and Master Plan for the Joint Survey and Demarcation of Land Boundary between the Kingdom of Thailand and the Kingdom of Cambodia”, p. 14. The JBC has since succeeded in delimiting some 600km of the border, with roughly 200km outstanding. 21 “Thai-Cambodian border row: Does 1:50,000 or 1:200,000 mapping give the edge?”, The Nation , 16 June 2025. In 2001, Bangkok and Phnom Penh signed a separate memorandum of understanding on overlapping maritime claims. Known as MOU 44, it provided for boundary delineation and joint development of hydrocarbons in a portion of the 26,000 sq km disputed area, which may contain as much as eleven trillion cubic feet of natural gas and between 300 and 500 million barrels of crude oil, with a combined value of some $300 billion. 22 “Memorandum of Understanding between the Government of the Kingdom of Thailand and the Government of the Kingdom of Cambodia regarding their Overlapping Maritime Claims to the Continental Shelf”, 18 June 2001; Supalak Ganjanakhundee, “Beyond scrapping the MOU: Navigating maritime disputes under UNCLOS”, Prachatai English , 1 June 2026. Appended to the document is a map depicting the two sides’ continental shelf claims and the resulting areas of overlap. This map has spurred criticism in Thailand as the Cambodian claim line appears to cross the island of Koh Kut, which the 1907 treaty had clearly identified as Siamese territory. C. Politics and Conflict The historical dispute over territory does not in itself explain why conflict erupted in 2025. Contemporary tension between the two countries is intimately linked to Thailand’s turbulent domestic politics, which for two decades has revolved around a contest for power between the tycoon-turned-politician Thaksin Shinawatra and his conservative opponents. 23 See Crisis Group Asia Reports N°274, Thailand’s Lengthening Roadmap to Elections , 10 December 2015; N°263, A Coup Ordained? Thailand’s Prospects for Stability , 3 December 2014; and N°192, Bridging Thailand’s Deep Divide , 5 July 2010; as well as Crisis Group Asia Briefings N°121, Thailand: The Calm before Another Storm? , 11 April 2011; N°82, Thailand: Calming the Political Turmoil , 22 September 2008; and N°80, Thailand: Political Turmoil and the Southern Insurgency , 28 August 2008. Thaksin also had close ties with Cambodia’s Hun Sen, who served as prime minister from 1985 to 2023, currently presides over the senate and still controls the ruling Cambodian People’s Party. That relationship crumbled in dramatic fashion in June 2025, with direct repercussions for bilateral relations. 1. Thailand Thaksin became prime minister in 2001. His Thai Rak Thai Party won support by delivering on popular policies but earned the enmity of conservatives and the military over alleged conflicts of interest and challenges to the prerogatives of the royal palace. Led by conservative royalists, the People’s Alliance for Democracy (PAD) took to the streets to call for Thaksin’s resignation in 2005. The military ousted him in a September 2006 coup, sending him into exile, but his proxy parties continued to win elections. The Thaksin/conservative divide was the fulcrum of Thai politics for more than a decade. In May 2008, under a Thaksin-aligned government, Thailand signed a joint communiqué with Cambodia supporting inscription of Preah Vihear temple as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The PAD promptly began using this issue as a cudgel against Thaksin, playing on the memory of the 1962 ICJ decision and the theme of lost territory, and portraying Thaksin’s purported business dealings in Cambodia as a threat to Thai sovereignty. 24 Crisis Group Report, Waging Peace , op. cit., pp. 4-5. Ever after, despite a lack of hard evidence of any conflict of interest, Thaksin’s opponents would accuse the Shinawatra family of “selling out” the national interest to Hun Sen. 25 Puangthong Pawakapan, State and Uncivil Society in Thailand at the Temple of Preah Vihear (Singapore, 2013), pp. 37, 62-64. With Preah Vihear [temple] ... a live political issue in Thailand, tensions increased on the border [with Cambodia]. With Preah Vihear again a live political issue in Thailand, tensions increased on the border. The two sides exchanged fire on six occasions between October 2008 and May 2011, claiming at least 34 lives. 26 Martin Wagener, “Lessons from Preah Vihear: Thailand, Cambodia and the Nature of Low-Intensity Border Conflicts”, Journal of Current Southeast Asian Affairs , vol. 30, no. 3 (2011), pp. 32-33. In April 2011, Cambodia requested that the ICJ interpret the 1962 verdict, particularly Thailand’s obligation to withdraw troops from the Preah Vihear temple or “its vicinity on Cambodian territory”. In July, the court issued a provisional ruling, including establishment of a demilitarised zone around Preah Vihear. In 2013, the ICJ affirmed Cambodia’s sovereignty over the promontory on which Preah Vihear is situated but referred delineation of the border in adjacent disputed territory to bilateral negotiations. “Request for interpretation of the Judgment of 15 June 1962 in the Case concerning the Temple of Preah Vihear (Cambodia v. Thailand) Request for the indication of provisional measures”, Summary of the Judgment, ICJ, 11 November 2013. In 2009, in a provocation to his political opponents, Thaksin accepted an appointment as an adviser to Hun Sen, who also offered refuge to his supporters fleeing a 2010 Thai army crackdown. Thaksin’s sister Yingluck, prime minister from 2011 to 2014, then took refuge in Cambodia after the Constitutional Court disqualified her from office, just before the military staged a coup. With the Thai military firmly in power and both Thaksin and Yingluck in exile, the pro/anti-Thaksin antagonism no longer defined Thai politics. But in 2023, the Thaksin-aligned Pheu Thai Party struck a bargain with its erstwhile conservative foes, joining forces to keep the progressive People’s Party from power after its massive general election victory. The deal allowed Thaksin proxy Srettha Thavisin to become prime minister and Thaksin himself to return home from fifteen years in exile. Hun Sen was Thaksin’s first visitor from abroad. 2. Cambodia Cambodia is ostensibly in transition from rule by Hun Sen to government by Hun Manet, who replaced his father as prime minister in 2023. During his 38 years as prime minister, Hun Sen consolidated power through a mix of co-optation and repression, while casting himself as Cambodia’s saviour. Beginning in 2017, a crackdown on dissent saw the main opposition party outlawed, scores of politicians jailed and driven into exile, and independent media suppressed. 27 Lee Morgenbesser, “Cambodia’s Transition to Hegemonic Authoritarianism”, Journal of Democracy , vol. 30, no. 1 (2019); Neil Loughlin, “Beyond Personalism: Elite Politics and Political Families in Cambodia”, Contemporary Southeast Asia , vol. 43, no. 2 (2021); “Cambodia: Hun Sen Extinguishes Media Freedom”, Human Rights Watch, 13 February 2023. Hun Sen remains extremely powerful, both as senate president and as the leading figure in the ruling Cambodian People’s Party (CPP). Hun Manet’s rise to the prime minister’s office is part of a generational succession designed to secure the Hun family’s pre-eminence by safeguarding the interests of other senior CPP figures; the sons of some of Hun Sen’s long-serving ministers took over their fathers’ posts at the same time. 28 Tea Banh, defence minister since 1993, handed down his position to his son Tea Seiha and Sar Kheng, interior minister since 1992, turned over his post to his son Sar Sokha. Hun Manet’s younger brothers also ascended to high-ranking positions. Will Brehm, “How did Hun Sen engineer a seamless succession in Cambodia?”, East Asia Forum , 9 September 2023. Unassuming and technocratic, Hun Manet appears focused on governance and economic reforms, but he governs in his father’s shadow, and it remains to be seen if he can keep Hun Sen’s coalition intact. 29 Crisis Group interview, former official, Phnom Penh, May 2026. See also Chheang Vannarith, “Hun Manet’s Worldview”, Southeast Asian Affairs 2025 (Singapore, 2025). While domestic political opposition is weak, Hun Sen appears worried about popular discontent. 30 Crisis Group interviews, diplomats and analysts, Phnom Penh, February 2026. The Hun family’s grip on power is not necessarily secure, as CPP factions weigh a post-Hun Sen future. 31 Crisis Group interviews, analysts, former official, Phnom Penh, February and May 2026. On 1 June, Hun Sen warned, “Only the ‘angels’ [CPP members] and their children have the right to govern this country”. 32 “Hun Sen warns extremists against ouster attempts”, Khmer Times , 3 June 2026. While Khmer nationalism has generally been the province of the CPP’s political opponents, confrontation with Thailand has offered Hun Sen an opportunity to burnish his own nationalist credentials and bolster his family’s political legitimacy during the period of generational succession. 33 Crisis Group interviews, analysts, Phnom Penh, February 2026. III. The Path to Conflict A convergence of heightened Thai nationalism, linked to conservatives’ antipathy for Thaksin, and escalatory actions by Cambodia, led to two rounds of fighting in 2025. A. The Resurgence of Thai Nationalism The unlikely bargain between Thaksin and conservative parties struck in 2023 to keep the progressive People’s Party from power set the stage for a revival of Thai nationalism anchored in anti-Cambodia sentiment. In February 2024, Prime Minister Srettha Thavisin agreed to open talks with Hun Manet on joint development of hydrocarbons in the maritime overlapping claims area, providing Thaksin’s opponents with a pretext to reopen the 2008 “lost territories” playbook. 34 “Thailand, Cambodia to discuss joint petroleum exploitation”, Bangkok Post , 7 February 2024. The refrain only grew stronger after Thaksin gave a speech that included a pledge to “unlock” the Gulf of Thailand’s oil and gas resources in August. 35 William J. Jones, “Thai nationalism rears its ugly head again”, East Asia Forum , 17 January 2025. Thaksin’s daughter Paetongtarn Shinawatra became prime minister in August 2024 and continued these nascent efforts, stirring the disquiet of conservatives and old PAD networks about MOU 44. 36 Thailand’s Constitutional Court removed Srettha Thavisin from office on 14 August 2024 for violating ethical standards in a cabinet appointment. Critics of the agreement argued that it jeopardised Thai sovereignty over the island of Koh Kut, conferred structural advantages upon Cambodia and reflected conflicts of interest on the Shinawatra clan’s part. 37 Tita Sanglee, “Doubt and Dissent: Thai Nationalist Views on the Thailand-Cambodia Maritime Dispute”, ISEAS Perspective , no. 9, 2025, p. 3. As a prominent Thaksin critic asked: “[F]or whose benefit is the Thai government rushing to negotiate within the old framework, given that [MOU 44] contradicts the 1973 Royal Decree [codifying Thailand’s continental shelf claim] and risks territorial loss, as in the Preah Vihear case?” 38 “‘Mom Korn’ points out that MOU 44 contradicts the royal decree of King Rama IX, risks losing territory and urges its immediate cancellation”, Thai Post , 25 October 2024 [Thai]. In June 2024, Paiboon Nititawan, deputy leader of the military-backed Phalang Pracharat Party (PPRP), petitioned the Constitutional Court to determine whether MOU 44 was illegal because parliament had not approved it. 39 “PPRP seeks ruling on MoU with Cambodia”, Bangkok Post , 14 June 2024. The court dismissed the petition in September of that year, on the grounds that Paiboon lacked the standing to bring such a case. 40 “Court verdict empowers Thai government to push energy deal with Cambodia”, Thai PBS World, 17 September 2024. The PPRP then held a press conference a month later alleging that joint development under MOU 44 could jeopardise Thailand’s sovereignty over Koh Kut, putting the government on the defensive. 41 “Thai territory bordering Cambodia is safe, says government”, Bangkok Post , 31 October 2024. Amid demands from the party and conservative activists to scrap MOU 44, Thailand’s defence minister visited the island to assert Thailand’s sovereignty. 42 “Thailand cannot scrap MOU 44 without Cambodia’s okay: Anutin”, The Nation , 4 November 2024; “Thai deputy PM makes case for Cambodia deal”, Bangkok Post , 9 November 2024. B. Border Tensions With maritime tensions simmering, friction increased along the land border. On 13 February 2025, a group of Cambodians visited the disputed Ta Muan Thom/Tamone Thom temple, reportedly escorted by Cambodian soldiers, and sang a patriotic song. Thai soldiers objected to the implicit assertion of sovereignty, which contradicted the “gentlemen’s agreement” governing the area since 2011, and asked the group to leave. 43 The arrangement permitted villagers from both nations to visit the temple but prohibited political or nationalist demonstrations. William J. Jones, “Cambodia undermines ASEAN centrality in 2025 border conflict”, Geopolitical Monitor , 29 January 2026. Video of the incident went viral. 44 “Thai-Cambodian tensions over anthem at temple”, Bangkok Post , 17 February 2025. Two weeks later, on 1 March, a pavilion in the Cambodia-Laos-Thailand tri-border area, built to commemorate neighbourly relations among the three countries, burned down. 45 “Thailand and Cambodia to discuss pavilion fire”, Bangkok Post , 6 March 2025. While the Thai military officially called it an accident, rumours circulated that Cambodian troops had set off the blaze. 46 Crisis Group interview, retired senior Thai military officer, Bangkok, June 2026. See also “Thailand and Cambodia to discuss pavilion fire”, op. cit. The situation escalated on 28 May, when Thai and Cambodian troops exchanged fire in a disputed area between Chong Bok in Thailand’s Ubon Ratchathani province and Cambodia’s Preah Vihear province, killing a Cambodian soldier; both sides claimed the other shot first. 47 “One killed after Thai and Cambodian soldiers briefly clash in a disputed border area”, Associated Press, 28 May 2025. A week earlier, Thailand had alleged that Cambodian troops had been digging trenches and building fortifications in disputed territory in the area but had agreed to withdraw after talks between local commanders. “Thai, Cambodian troops hold talks over border patrol dispute”, The Nation , 18 May 2025. Prime Minister Paetongtarn spoke to Hun Manet the same day. “We don’t want this to escalate”, she told the media. 48 “Paetongtarn discusses with Hun Manet after Thai-Cambodian border clash”, The Nation , 29 May 2025. The countries’ army chiefs met two days later and agreed to pull back their troops. 49 “Army chiefs try to resolve Thai-Cambodian border dispute”, Bangkok Post , 30 May 2025. A welter of developments ensued in June. On 4 June, more than a week after the clash with Cambodian troops, Paetongtarn’s government released a statement affirming “unwavering commitment to safeguarding sovereignty and territorial integrity”. 50 “Statement by Thai Government on Thailand-Cambodia Border Situation”, Thai Government Public Relations Department, 4 June 2025; “Thailand, Cambodia mobilise troops, evacuate villages”, The Nation , 5 June 2025.
