The U.S. and UN Will Need More Patience to Resolve Western Sahara Conflict cmoore Fri, 10/09/2026 - 17:45 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List A United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) Mil Mi-8 helicopter lands on the Moroccan side of the border crossing point between Morocco and Mauritania, in Guerguerat located in the Western Sahara. 25 November, 2020. AFP / Fadel Senna Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 09 October 2026 17 minutes The U.S. and UN Will Need More Patience to Resolve Western Sahara Conflict Talks between Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front over Western Sahara have hit a wall, with U.S. and UN representatives pushing for Rabat’s autonomy plan as the centrepiece of negotiations. If they are to broker a compromise, the mediators will have to slow down. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Arabic English Arabic Riccardo Fabiani Project Director, North Africa https://twitter.com/ricfabiani Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy Western Sahara Morocco Mauritania For some time after October 2025, it seemed that the long diplomatic stalemate over Western Sahara might have been broken. This desert territory is claimed by Morocco but sought by the Algeria-based Polisario Front as the home of an independent state for the Sahrawi people. A UN Security Council resolution passed in October 2025 strengthened international backing for a Moroccan autonomy proposal while remaining vague enough to allow for the possibility of other outcomes. Working together with the UN envoy to Western Sahara, Washington used this narrow opening to bring Morocco and the Polisario back into direct discussions for the first time since 2019. Algeria and Mauritania, both neighbours of Western Sahara, also joined. Three rounds of talks in Washington and Madrid allowed the parties to explore practical elements of a possible settlement without forcing either Morocco or the Polisario to abandon its stance on Western Sahara’s sovereignty, autonomy and self-determination. But the opening is now in danger of closing. The U.S. and UN tried to move too fast, from exploratory discussions to negotiations centred on Morocco’s autonomy proposal, meeting with firm resistance from the Polisario, which insists on a self-determination vote. Meanwhile, a series of diplomatic and military incidents sullied what had been a constructive atmosphere. Washington has responded by applying increasing pressure on the Front, entertaining alternative Sahrawi interlocutors and considering changes to the diplomatic framework. Uncertainty about the U.S. position on the future of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) adds another complication. The U.S. concededly has a difficult diplomatic task. It needs to show both resolve and a capacity for patience if it wants to coax the parties toward progress – and right now the balance is off. Why the U.S. decided to become so seized of this issue is unclear, but if the objective is a quick diplomatic win, then it is looking at the wrong file. Indeed, there is a significant risk that, if the administration persists in trying to force a quick settlement, it will risk deepening the mistrust that has long impeded progress in negotiations. Rather than searching for shortcuts, the U.S. and UN should seek to rebuild confidence among the parties, preserve an open negotiating framework and gradually create the political conditions under which substantive compromises might eventually become possible. Creating Space for Talks The Western Sahara conflict dates to 1975, when Spain withdrew from the territory and Morocco and Mauritania moved to divide it between them. The Polisario Front, backed principally by Algeria, launched an armed struggle for independence. Thousands of Sahrawis fled to Algeria. A UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991 envisaged a referendum on self-determination, but disagreements over who should be able to vote have prevented it from taking place. Morocco has instead promoted a plan that would devolve powers to an autonomous Western Sahara under Rabat’s sovereignty, while the Polisario continues to demand a route to independence. The ceasefire collapsed in 2020, though fighting has remained limited. That same year, during President Donald Trump’s first term, the U.S. recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara, in exchange for Morocco’s normalisation of relations with Israel; during Trump’s second term, the administration has strongly endorsed Rabat’s autonomy plan. In October 2025, the UN Security Council agreed to renew MINURSO’s mandate for another year, with new language more explicitly supporting Morocco’s autonomy plan. As the penholder, the U.S. had tabled a first draft that called autonomy “the basis” for future negotiations and “the most feasible solution”; but consultations among Council members led to watered-down language. The final version’s ambiguously (and awkwardly) worded text says autonomy will be taken “as basis” for negotiations and represents “a most feasible solution”. The Council thus gave its strong backing for the autonomy plan, while leaving the door ajar for discussion of other proposals. While both the Polisario and Algeria said the resolution’s final version improved upon the first draft, they rejected it. While both the Polisario and Algeria said the resolution’s final version improved upon the first draft, they rejected it. The former reiterated its demand for a self-determination referendum to settle the conflict, while the latter – then an elected member of the Council – took the politically unsurprising but exceptionally rare step of not voting on the resolution to register its opposition to a reference to “Moroccan sovereignty” in one of its preambular clauses. Nonetheless, U.S. Senior Advisor for Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos used the resolution’s ambiguity to press Algeria and the Polisario to return to negotiations. In the weeks after the Council vote, Boulos signalled to both actors that, though Washington clearly supported autonomy, the UN resolution did not preclude another solution if the conflict parties agreed to it. At the time, a Polisario official told Crisis Group that “Boulos’s language is more neutral than the UN Security Council resolution” – an expression of growing confidence in Washington’s role. Between January and February 2026, ministerial-level delegations from Algeria, Mauritania, Morocco and the Polisario gathered twice in Washington and once in Madrid, the first direct meetings between the conflict parties in seven years. The co-chairs were Boulos, U.S. Ambassador to the UN Michael Waltz and UN envoy Staffan de Mistura. These rounds differed from previous efforts in at least three ways. First, Washington was directly involved in the discussions, marking a break from its traditional role as the UN envoy’s external supporter, with U.S. officials both driving the conversation and giving de Mistura space to help do the same. Secondly, Algeria and Mauritania participated in the talks – though only as ostensible “observers”. For years, Rabat has wanted Algiers and Nouakchott involved in negotiations, claiming that the Polisario is an Algerian proxy and that, to be durable, any agreement will have to be part of a grand bargain with countries abutting Western Sahara. Algeria and Mauritania have countered that they are merely neighbours interested in the conflict’s resolution (hence their insistence on “observer” status). Thirdly, ahead of the talks and responding to a demand repeatedly put forward by the U.S. and its European partners over the years, Morocco expanded its four-page autonomy proposal floated in 2007 into a comprehensive 40-page blueprint to guide negotiations. The co-chairs insisted on confidentiality from the participants to protect discussions from political pressures at home. Though news broke that the four parties were talking, the contents of the three rounds have remained mostly secret, with Morocco’s expanded autonomy plan still under wraps. That said, diplomatic sources have told Crisis Group that the talks, which apparently touched upon organising elections and reintegrating Sahrawi refugees, among other things, went well overall. In a conversation with Crisis Group, a Polisario official was keen to stress that these exchanges were “a discussion, not a negotiation”. The open-ended format seemed to suit both sides, making it possible for them to re-engage with each other, however warily. From Progress to Stalemate The talks subsequently hit a wall, however. After the three meetings, the U.S. and UN repeatedly asked the Front to offer its comments on Rabat’s plan with the aim of kickstarting a more substantive discussion of how to end the conflict. The Polisario baulked, with an official explaining to Crisis Group that the Front “has not accepted the Moroccan autonomy plan as the basis for negotiations and the UN Security Council does not require us to accept it”. While this position should not have been surprising – the talks gained momentum only because of the ambiguity that the U.S. had managed to create around this key issue – U.S. and UN diplomats seemed both frustrated and bewildered by the Front’s attitude. A U.S. official noted that “Algeria showed much more flexibility than the Polisario” by encouraging the Front to respond to Morocco’s autonomy plan, rather than rejecting the proposal out of hand. Between May and June, relations between the parties – as well as between the U.S. and the Polisario – quickly deteriorated. On 5 May, after a long period of quiet, the Front fired rockets at the city of Smara, in Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara, wounding a civilian and damaging a number of buildings. The U.S., France and several other countries, along with the EU and UN, immediately condemned the attack, calling it an attempt to undermine negotiations . The next day, U.S. Ambassador to Morocco Duke Buchan III visited Dakhla, in Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara, reiterating the Trump administration’s recognition of Rabat’s sovereignty and criticising the Polisario. On 7 May, the Polisario issued a statement denouncing Buchan’s visit and justifying the Smara attack as legitimate resistance to colonialism. Things took a turn for the worse after an exchange of letters between Ambassador Waltz and Polisario leaders failed to restore mutual confidence. Things took a turn for the worse after an exchange of letters between Ambassador Waltz and Polisario leaders failed to restore mutual confidence. According to several U.S. and European diplomats, Waltz wrote to ask whether the Front’s leaders were still committed to a negotiated solution after Smara. The Polisario reportedly responded with a long missive about the dispute’s complexity that Washington saw as obfuscatory. At that point, a number of administration insiders turned against the group. Tensions escalated further when, on 7 June, Moroccan forces killed Lahbib Abdelaziz, son of former Polisario leader Mohamed Abdelaziz and a potential future leader of the Front. His killing shocked pro-independence Sahrawis, who complained that (in contrast to the outcry that followed the Smara attack) there was precious little international condemnation. Then, on 8 June, Sahrawi activist Naama Asfari – who was arrested in 2010 in connection with protests at Gdeim Izik – began a hunger strike , which lasted 47 days and ended only after Rabat granted him a transfer to a jail closer to his family. By late June, U.S. frustration with the Polisario had begun to show. On 30 June, Waltz met with a delegation of the Sahrawi Movement for Peace (MSP), founded in 2020 as a self-styled moderate alternative to the Polisario, expressing willingness to negotiate with Morocco over autonomy. Waltz praised the MSP as an organisation committed to “peace, compromise and a durable solution” that “the world should hear”. Another meeting between a U.S. embassy official and an MSP delegation followed on 28 July. With these steps, the U.S. was breaking with a well-established practice of recognising the Polisario as the representative of the Sahrawi people (even if there was some dispute over whether it should be considered the sole, exclusive representative) and raising the spectre that it might bypass the Front absent greater cooperation. The Front reacted dismissively. A Polisario official told Crisis Group that U.S. officials “should come on the ground and see who really represents the Sahrawis. The Polisario comes from the people and remains representative. The groups they want to promote are nothing”. Summing up the U.S. approach, a Western diplomat told Crisis Group that Washington believes the Polisario’s choice is between “the hard way and the harder way”, meaning that continued resistance by the movement to engaging with Morocco’s plan will bring more adverse consequences upon it. In another sign of tougher steps to come, and in parallel to the talks, a group of U.S. members of Congress introduced two bills that would require the Secretary of State to designate the Polisario as a foreign terrorist organisation (FTO) due to its alleged links with Iran and Lebanese Hizbollah. For legal and political reasons, it is hard to imagine these bills passing into law and being enforced, and the administration has expressed no support for them. But the administration could be working with Congressional allies to signal what might come next should the impasse persist. Searching for Alternatives Faced with a diplomatic deadlock ahead of the expiry of MINURSO’s mandate at the end of October, U.S. officials have been weighing other options, including replacing the Polisario with more flexible Sahrawi representatives, such as the MSP, in the talks. A Western diplomat observed that Washington could use the mandate renewal to try including new language that creates space at the negotiating table for the MSP and others (eg, elected Sahrawi officials who reside in Morocco) – for instance by referring to “Sahrawi representatives” rather than “the Polisario Front” when describing the concerned parties. That said, not all U.S. officials seem ready to drop the Front or give up on the current format. In a 25 September interview with France 24 , Boulos stressed that the U.S. was still hoping the Polisario would engage in talks, praised Algeria’s stance and highlighted that more work was needed to achieve a mutually acceptable settlement. The pro-Polisario media welcomed these remarks. In his 28 September speech to the UN General Assembly, Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf reiterated his country’s rejection of any shortcut to a deal: “Algeria warns that any attempt to bypass this framework of reference or marginalise the holders of the inalienable right, the people of Western Sahara and their sole, legitimate representative, the Polisario Front, will not contribute to resolving the conflict; rather, it will further exacerbate tensions”. Meanwhile, Morocco has been assiduously currying favour with the Trump administration, even if it has not openly backed the idea of opening negotiations to other Sahrawi groups. In July, King Mohamed VI announced that the Tiznit-Dakhla road connecting Morocco to Western Sahara would be renamed the Donald J. Trump Highway as “a personal expression of my high regard”. On 15 September, Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and U.S. Ambassador Waltz agreed in New York on upgrading Israel-Morocco relations by appointing ambassadors and working toward a series of economic agreements to be signed by year’s end. In their official statement, the three countries reaffirmed Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara and support for the autonomy plan. “The tripartite agreement with the U.S. and Israel is an essential part of Morocco’s approach to Western Sahara”, a Moroccan expert told Crisis Group. “The diplomatic upgrade is a gesture addressed to Washington, as we need the U.S. on our side ahead of the next Security Council meeting”. According to Moroccan and European sources, Rabat is hoping that the MINURSO renewal will, among other things, include clearer backing for the autonomy plan as “the only basis” for resolving the conflict. MINURSO’s future remains up in the air. At this stage, MINURSO’s future remains up in the air. In October 2025, Washington tried to shorten the mission’s mandate to three months, hoping that more frequent Security Council involvement might increase pressure on the parties to reach a deal, thus allowing MINURSO to wind down, in line with the U.S. agenda of reducing spending on peacekeeping missions. Eventually, the U.S. settled for a twelve-month renewal in parallel with a strategic review conducted by the Secretary-General. Meanwhile, in anticipation of U.S. requests to trim peacekeeping spending, MINURSO underwent cuts , removing 23 civilian posts, reducing flying hours and slashing its own budget by 11.5 per cent. In an April Senate hearing , Waltz mentioned MINURSO as a mission that – in the Trump administration’s eyes – has outlived its purpose. Several European diplomats told Crisis Group that they suspected Washington would once again push for a major cut in the mission’s expenses or (less likely) its termination during the next renewal debate. MINURSO’s political mandate has changed beyond recognition since its inception, insofar as it presently plays only a marginal role in diplomacy. But European officials who spoke to Crisis Group share the conviction that its presence remains critical to avoiding escalation. In 2022, Morocco made clear that, should MINURSO withdraw from the UN buffer zone separating the territory held by Rabat from the Algerian and Mauritanian borders, the kingdom would occupy this strip of land. If that were to happen, the Polisario would likely attack Moroccan installations from Algeria or Mauritania, rather than using the buffer zone as its launchpad, as is now the case. In turn, Rabat might decide to pursue Polisario units into Algerian or Mauritanian territory, potentially dragging its neighbours into conflict. Rebuilding Confidence among the Parties With the October deadline for renewing the MINURSO mandate fast approaching, U.S. officials could be tempted to either strong-arm the Polisario into accepting Morocco’s autonomy plan or replace the Front with a more accommodating alternative. They may hope that this small organisation will eventually buckle under Washington’s pressure, fearful of the consequences of continued obduracy, which might range from being cast aside to being designated as an FTO, with the severe attendant sanctions. For an administration keen to secure quick deals to end wars, ending the Western Sahara conflict might look like low-hanging fruit. Taking this tack would be highly risky. Since the breakdown of the UN-organised referendum scheme in the early 2000s and, in particular, the resumption of hostilities in 2020, confidence between Morocco and the Polisario has been running low, a by-product of the conflict’s five-decade duration, the accumulation of failed diplomatic initiatives, competing legal and historical narratives, and repeated periods of military confrontation and political deadlock. The two sides continue to approach negotiations from fundamentally different premises: Morocco sees autonomy under its sovereignty as the sole viable end state, while the Polisario insists on a process that preserves the option of independence. In addition, since the 2021 diplomatic rupture between Algeria and Morocco, the conflict has been nestled within a regional dispute , further complicating efforts to resolve it. U.S. pressure alone is unlikely to yield a substantive breakthrough, certainly not without simultaneous confidence-building measures. U.S. pressure alone is unlikely to yield a substantive breakthrough, certainly not without simultaneous confidence-building measures. The Polisario regards self-determination for all practical purposes as an existential issue, meaning that it is more likely to dig in than concede in the face of coercion, with much of the cost of any standoff being borne by vulnerable Sahrawi refugees. In such a scenario, the risk of escalatory violence would also increase. For leaders on both sides to make difficult concessions, and for public opinion to accept them, at least some preliminary steps are needed. Otherwise, both will view negotiations as a zero-sum game, dimming prospects for a resolution. “We need a minimum of trust”, a Polisario official commented to Crisis Group. Against this backdrop, Washington should drop any illusion of reaching a swift deal. Instead, it ought to embrace a more patient approach that, for now, focuses on clearing the air among parties whose relations have soured. The co-chairs should look to four confidence-building measures that might create a better atmosphere for future talks. They should: First, press Morocco and the Polisario to allow Sahrawi families in Algerian refugee camps to visit Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara, and vice versa, resuming a program that was suspended in 2014. These exchanges would create regular, low-risk cooperation among Morocco, Polisario and the UN in service of a concrete humanitarian need, while reconnecting people divided by the conflict and helping reduce both mistrust and the political cost of engagement; Secondly, urge Morocco to release some or all the Sahrawi prisoners it has held since the 2010 Gdeim Izik protests – or at least to honour prisoners’ requests for transfer to jails closer to their families; Thirdly, push the Polisario to declare a unilateral truce in return. Even though the Front rejects returning to the 1991 ceasefire, it might be persuaded to temporarily suspend its attacks to avoid undermining talks; and Finally, arrange for U.S. and UN officials to visit the Sahrawi refugee camps in Tindouf, Algeria, meeting the Polisario leadership and holding town hall-style meetings with refugees to listen to their concerns. The co-chairs also should revise their diplomatic approach to get out of the current cul-de-sac. Rather than pushing the Polisario to respond to Morocco’s autonomy plan – which it rejects as a sole basis for negotiations – they should revert to the format of the three rounds held in Washington and Madrid, thus creating space for the parties to continue a less structured exchange of views on their respective plans. The co-chairs could facilitate these conversations and advance bridging proposals on the specific issues discussed. The most difficult questions relating to sovereignty should be left for the end. Over time, such an approach – pursued on the basis that “nothing is agreed until everything is agreed” – might eventually allow for more in-depth discussions. Algeria has made clear it would not participate in a dialogue that does not include the [Polisario] Front. Crucially, the U.S. should stop suggesting it might replace the Polisario with other Sahrawi representatives in the talks. Algeria has made clear it would not participate in a dialogue that does not include the Front. Besides, any settlement reached with such alternative groups would almost certainly lack popular buy-in and would fuel tensions among Morocco, the Polisario, Algeria and Mauritania. That said, the co-chairs might create a purely consultative parallel track bringing together other Sahrawis, from elected officials in Morocco to the MSP to civil society groups from the Tindouf camps – all of whom might have more political flexibility to put ideas on the table than Morocco and the Polisario. These Sahrawis could contribute their ideas on specific issues such as elections, natural resource management and refugee reintegration – as well as on the sovereignty-related endgame issues. For its part, the Polisario should engage more earnestly in the process. Whatever the Front thinks of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign, both the Polisario and Sahrawi refugees would benefit from seeing it defused. Showing some flexibility would have the dual advantage of helping stave off this threat while taking advantage of U.S. engagement to advance diplomacy. For example, the Polisario could present a new proposal based on a 2003 plan advanced by James Baker, the former U.S. secretary of state who was then UN envoy. Under that plan, which combined autonomy and self-determination, Western Sahara would have had five years of substantial self-rule, with an elected local executive and legislature, while Morocco would have retained responsibility for foreign affairs and defence. After that transitional period, the UN would have held a referendum on the territory’s final status. At the time, the Front accepted the plan, while Rabat rejected it. Such a counteroffer would at least provide the co-chairs with a document they could use in trying to bridge the gap between the two sides’ positions. Morocco should also find ways to show flexibility. While one concrete way to do that might be releases of Gdeim Izik prisoners, it will also need to set something of a different tone in negotiations, resisting the temptation to treat autonomy as an outcome that can be fast-tracked. A more durable settlement will require Rabat to accept a long, difficult negotiating process in which trust gradually is rebuilt and the terms of any eventual compromise are worked through with the Polisario, rather than presented as a fait accompli . Meanwhile, the UN Security Council should refrain from sunsetting MINURSO and ensure that any effort to streamline its mandate or reform the mission preserves its military monitoring component to manage the risk that fighting will spill into Algerian or Mauritanian territory. Washington may reasonably seek to review the mission’s costs and functions, but reforms that significantly weaken or eliminate this military role could remove one of the few remaining stabilising mechanisms in Western Sahara. Finally, Washington should maintain a balanced approach to regional diplomacy – engaging regularly with both Algeria and Morocco, as it has sought to do during the current diplomatic effort, rather than allowing its closer ties with Rabat to feed perceptions that it is taking sides in an increasingly polarised regional competition. Maintaining credible channels with both capitals could help contain bilateral tensions, limit the Western Sahara dispute’s entanglement in wider rivalries and protect the political space needed for an eventual negotiated settlement. Should U.S. diplomats instead choose to intensify pressure on the Polisario and its backers in hopes of forcing rapid acceptance of Morocco’s autonomy framework, they are likely to find – potentially at high cost to the parties and to the region – that a conflict more than five decades old is unlikely to be resolved through coercion alone. A Fateful Choice: Will This Election Change Israel? cmoore Mon, 10/12/2026 - 13:35 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List A Fateful Choice: Will This Election Change Israel? Online Event Tuesday, 20 October 2026 10am Washington, DC | 4pm Brussels | 5pm Tel Aviv Please register here if you would like to attend this online event. The Knesset elections on 27 October could be the most consequential in Israel’s short history. After four years of hard-right government under Benjamin Netanyahu, and three years of war on multiple fronts since the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, Israelis head to the polls with starkly different hopes for their future. About a dozen political parties are expected to cross the threshold needed to enter the 120-seat parliament. Two main blocs, of nearly equal weight according to polls, face off against each other: an alliance of hard-right parties dominated by Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister and head of the Likud party, and an opposing camp led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff and head of Yashar, a centre-right party he founded last year. A third group, made up of parties that represent Israel’s Palestinian minority, is projected to capture a smaller but critical share of seats. Whichever bloc comes out on top, a question hangs over the vote: has the Israeli political “centre” shifted so much that even new leaders may not bring real change – at least, not on big issues that matter to the rest of the world, such as accommodating the 7.5 million Palestinians that live under Israeli rule? In this online event, Crisis Group brings together leading Israeli political analysts who will tackle this and other questions. Pulling Ethiopia and Eritrea Back from War cmoore Mon, 10/12/2026 - 21:44 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Members of the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) gather in front of Mekelle Alula Aba Nega International Airport after federal forces retook control of the facility in Mekelle on 6 October, 2026 AFP Alert / Africa 12 October 2026 11 minutes Pulling Ethiopia and Eritrea Back from War Addis Ababa and Asmara are edging closer to a direct conflict, which would cause further mayhem in the troubled Horn of Africa and the Red Sea basin. It is not too late to avert disaster. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Ethiopia Eritrea Horn of Africa Ethiopia and Eritrea stand perilously close to all-out war as heavy fighting inches close to their shared border. The threat of resurgent interstate conflict in the Horn of Africa follows several weeks of fighting between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which launched an armed rebellion on 23 September. The Ethiopian military has gained the upper hand in those clashes, moving northward after capturing Tigray’s regional capital, Mekelle, on 3 October. Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF and deploying military personnel on its soil, a claim that has been backed up by media reports and other accounts, though it appears that Eritrea subsequently pulled its troops back toward the border in the face of an Ethiopian advance and reported drones strikes on its forces. The effects of these cross-border movements could be dire: they could trigger a full-scale war between Ethiopia and Eritrea that, in turn, could spiral into a wider conflagration along Eritrea’s Red Sea coast. A push at the highest political and diplomatic levels to prevent this budding confrontation is a matter of extreme urgency. The Resurgence of Conflict The risk of direct conflict between Ethiopia and Eritrea has risen sharply since late September as war has engulfed Tigray. On 20 September, the TPLF and six other groups announced a new “alliance for survival” aimed at toppling Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government, which they see as authoritarian and bent on centralising power. Two days later, Ethiopia conducted a large drone raid on sites in southern Tigray, where officials believed the TPLF was massing for an attack. On 23 September, the TPLF mounted large-scale offensives against the federal government. It was apparently trying to join forces with two of its allies, the Amhara Fano and Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front, which commenced their own assaults on Ethiopian military positions near Tigray’s boundaries. This first wave of attacks made gains, but Ethiopian forces quickly regrouped. They have steadily pushed the Tigrayans back since then, recording a string of battlefield victories and capturing most of Tigray. On 3 October, federal forces and their allies took Mekelle without a fight. As the TPLF withdrew, the war’s front line shifted toward the group’s strongholds in the northern mountains, near the border with Eritrea. At the same time, tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea reached fever pitch in the wake of reported Eritrean troop deployments to northern Tigray in support of the TPLF’s rear guard. For the first time since 2000, when Ethiopia and Eritrea ended their last war, the two neighbours now seem poised to engage in frontal combat. For the first time since 2000, when Ethiopia and Eritrea ended their last war, the two neighbours now seem poised to engage in frontal combat. Frictions between the two are neither sudden nor surprising, even if the present rift between them in some ways marks a radical turnaround. For more than a year, Addis Ababa has been denouncing Asmara, and more recently its allies in the Sudanese army, for backing rebel groups in Ethiopia, particularly the TPLF. This antagonism stands in sharp contrast to what prevailed during the last Tigray war, which raged between 2020 and 2022, when Ethiopia and Eritrea had become friends rather than foes. That conflict came on the heels of Abiy’s ascent to power, which in turn dethroned the TPLF, a pivotal force in national politics for decades, and set the stage for a power struggle between the federal government and the TPLF high command in Tigray. Eritrea, which had fought its previous war with Ethiopia from 1998 to 2000 while the TPLF was in charge in Addis Ababa, sought common cause with Abiy in confronting the group after Tigrayan forces attacked Ethiopia’s Northern Command in November 2020. A seesaw battle ensued, with Addis Ababa and its allies eventually beating back the TPLF ahead of the signing of the Pretoria peace agreement in November 2022. This agreement left the TPLF largely intact, however, and its commitment to fully demobilise its armed forces was never fully enforced. Eritrea, which was not involved in the Pretoria negotiations, had been pushing for the group’s complete elimination. Asmara was incensed at the outcome. In its view, its critical national interests had not been respected during the talks. Eritrea’s relations with Ethiopia subsequently began to deteriorate. Some say Abiy was quietly courting the TPLF in order to establish a new alliance with it against Eritrea in the acrimonious aftermath of the peace deal. TPLF leaders apparently rebuffed these advances. Abiy also began to argue in public that Ethiopia needed to restore sovereign access to the sea. He said Ethiopia had a historical claim to the Red Sea coastline, which it had lost when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Since then, Ethiopia, the world’s largest landlocked country by population size, has been relying almost exclusively on Djibouti to export goods by sea. Officials in Abiy’s government have stressed that Ethiopia will not be satisfied merely with access to a wider range of ports, a course some have suggested it pursue, but needs a sovereign seaboard with a naval base. Asmara has viewed this rhetoric as a threat to seize Eritrea’s coastline, especially its southern port of Assab, by armed force. With bilateral relations souring, Eritrea and the TPLF began to explore establishing a common front against Addis Ababa. With bilateral relations souring, Eritrea and the TPLF began to explore establishing a common front against Addis Ababa. Asmara appears to have seen Tigray in the TPLF’s grip as a potential geographic buffer between it and the Ethiopian heartland, as well as a military counterweight to Addis Ababa. The TPLF, for its part, was keen to break the encirclement it endured in the 2020-2022 war. As a sign of their strengthening ties, Eritrean and Tigrayan authorities promoted new cross-border “people-to-people” exchanges known as tsimdo (“engagement” in Tigrinya), providing further ballast for their switch from adversaries to allies. Meanwhile, the 2022 peace deal began to fray. The TPLF complained that the government had failed to resolve major issues stemming from the conflict, including the status of disputed territories occupied by Amhara forces during the war and the return of displaced people to their homes in these areas. Little effort was made to remedy the antipathy between the TPLF and Abiy: Addis Ababa never reintegrated Tigray back into the national political federation, with the region remaining without representation in parliament or other institutions in the capital. In March 2025, the TPLF ousted the first post-war interim Tigray administrator, Getachew Reda, who had been a lead negotiator in the Pretoria peace negotiations for the TPLF and was chosen ahead of TPLF chairperson Debretsion Gebremichael. The group claimed that Getachew was too close to the federal government and had not defended Tigray’s interests sufficiently during his time in office. (Getachew fled to Addis Ababa, where he joined Abiy’s administration.) Abiy then appointed Tadesse Werede, a top Tigrayan general, in Getachew’s place, but the relationship between Tigray’s new ruler and the TPLF also began to worsen. In May 2026, the TPLF retook power in Mekelle, dismantling the interim administration, reinstalling its leader Debretsion as regional president and placing Tadesse under house arrest. The federal government responded by tightening its economic restrictions on the region and launching a campaign of airstrikes inside Tigray. In August, a major clash broke out between TPLF and federal ground forces before quickly subsiding. Shuttle diplomacy by the African Union and others aimed at restarting negotiations failed to gain traction. Simultaneously, mediators found their efforts thwarted by rising hostility among powers across the Horn. Addis Ababa began to denounce Asmara for trying to coordinate a transnational alliance against it, and accused the Sudanese army , an ally of Eritrea and Egypt (another Ethiopian foe), of supporting meetings of a nascent alliance of opposition groups in eastern Sudan. Ethiopia also complained that Sudan was harbouring a group of Tigrayan troops, known as Army 70, in Sudanese territory, where they were said to have stood alongside the army in fighting its enemy, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Ethiopia, on the other hand, began allowing the RSF to base itself in its Benishangul-Gumuz region close to the Sudanese border, from where it could launch attacks into Sudan’s Blue Nile state. Ethiopia’s relations with the Sudanese army, which had continued to function despite the chill between them, became icy as a result. Sudan has also claimed that drones attacking Khartoum were dispatched from Ethiopian territory. Neighbours at Loggerheads This mosaic of enmities and alliances has come into sharp relief since war broke out in Tigray. As hostilities have intensified, Ethiopia and Eritrea have edged ever closer to conflict. Ethiopia considers Eritrea to be masterminding the TPLF’s war effort. Soon after fighting broke out, Ethiopian federal officials and Afar’s regional president accused Eritrea of deploying forces in the Afar region. On 1 October, Ethiopia expelled all Eritrean diplomats from the country, accusing Asmara of “direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence”. All diplomatic ties between the two states have since been severed. After Ethiopian federal forces began advancing north of Mekelle, the first reports emerged of alleged Eritrean deployments in northern Tigray, seemingly with the aim of bolstering the TPLF’s defensive lines. Several media reports indicated on 7 October that Eritrean units had passed through Adigrat, 30km south of the Ethiopian border. Accounts also suggest that Eritrean forces took up positions south of Adigrat in the Edaga Hamus area. A day later, after reported drone strikes on Eritrean vehicles, some of its forces reportedly withdrew to the border. With Ethiopian forces currently approaching the frontier at several points, the two armies are positioned in alarmingly close proximity. Asmara’s apparent gamble to intervene more directly in the war, even if the incursion was brief, could well backfire. On 9 October, Ethiopia wrote a letter to the UN Security Council saying it was “taking measures” of self-defence in response to Eritrea’s deployment of infantry and mechanised units across the border and occupation of Ethiopian territory. The letter also accused Eritrea of “harbouring, supporting, financing, arming and directing armed insurgent groups operating within Ethiopia”. On 10 October, Eritrea responded with its own letter, accusing Ethiopia of declaring a “war of aggression” against it three years ago and using self-defence as a pretext for acts of war. The Security Council has scheduled a closed-door session to discuss the crisis on 13 October. A standoff along the two countries’ frontier would be an ominous turn of events. A standoff along the two countries’ frontier would be an ominous turn of events. The last major interstate conflict in the Horn of Africa, in which hundreds of thousands perished in trench warfare, was fought along precisely the same border. One flashpoint could be Eritrean military positions inside Ethiopian territory; another could be disputed territory along the border. Should Eritrean forces fully withdraw to their side of the border, Ethiopia could point to Eritrea’s apparent incursion and alleged harbouring of TPLF fighters as justification for seeking to cross into Eritrea. Even if Ethiopia stops short of a land invasion of Eritrea (and Ethiopian officials maintain that they have no intention of fighting a war on Eritrean soil), aerial warfare using drones and other long-range strike weapons could cause devastating harm. Ethiopia possesses the larger air force and drone arsenal, and it could try to quickly overwhelm Eritrea’s air defences. Should the two states lock horns, war could also extend across the region. The Sudanese army and Egypt look primed to jump to Eritrea’s defence, though it is uncertain how much support they would be willing or able to give. On the other side, the United Arab Emirates could be expected to back Ethiopia with more arms transfers. Saudi Arabia is keen to prevent a new front from emerging along the Red Sea, especially one involving the UAE, and has tried in the past to de-escalate tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea. On this occasion, however, Riyadh might be tempted to throw its weight behind Eritrea should a larger conflict erupt, given that its own Red Sea security would be at stake. That said, Saudi Arabia is also embroiled in a fresh round of fighting in Yemen and may not want to rally to the side of what might be a losing cause. Halting the Slide to War Pulling Ethiopia and Eritrea back from the brink of war should be the priority for all those interested in preventing a deadly chain of interconnected conflicts from snaking across the Horn of Africa and Red Sea regions. Capitals such as Washington, Nairobi, Pretoria, London, Paris, Rome, Riyadh, Ankara and Abu Dhabi should press both sides to avoid escalation. In particular, they should urge Abiy to refrain from advancing into Eritrean territory. They should also appeal to Asmara to respect Ethiopian sovereignty and withdraw any remaining troops from Ethiopian territory, should they still be stationed there. Despite their rift, Saudi Arabia and the UAE could also use this moment to work together to staunch a new conflict along the Red Sea, which could otherwise cause even more trouble in their bilateral relations. Should efforts to avert an outright war prevail, diplomats should not desist until they manage to achieve a durable de-escalation of tensions between the two capitals. The heart of any settlement between the two countries is likely to be respect for each other’s sovereignty and restoration of diplomatic ties. In focusing on calming regional tensions, mediators should not forget the dispute between the Ethiopian government and the TPLF, should the latter manage to avoid complete collapse following its reversals. African leaders still look best placed to restart the Tigray peace track, even if neither federal officials nor TPLF leaders appear ready for direct talks any time soon. Prior to the start of hostilities, former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, who oversaw the Pretoria negotiations that ended the last Tigray war, had been acting as the African Union’s peace envoy for the region. He visited Addis Ababa and Mekelle several times earlier in the year but had little success in bringing the two sides together. Efforts should be made to reactivate Obasanjo at the earliest opportunity. Other African leaders or ex-leaders could also be dispatched, such as South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, who made a quick stop in Addis Ababa on 5 October to speak with Abiy, or former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta, who also played a key role in the Pretoria negotiations in 2022. The U.S. or European powers could also play a part behind the scenes in trying to rekindle peace talks. At a minimum, all sides should press the federal government and the TPLF to abide by humanitarian commitments under international law. The UN Security Council, which as noted will discuss the crisis on 13 October, should make a clear call for both sides to respect the UN Charter and instruct the Secretary-General to undertake urgent diplomacy to prevent a new war between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Another war in the Horn of Africa may lie around the corner. Outright conflict between Ethiopia and Eritrea would likely spread to the Red Sea, disrupting the African side of this strategic waterway. It could also prove to be yet another front in the Horn that is easy to open and hard to close, especially once it becomes entangled in the mesh of disputes among neighbours and across the region. The best time to stop the looming Ethiopia-Eritrea war is now, before any more damage is done. War’s Hidden Mental Health Toll on Children with Disabilities. Click to expand Image Ibrahim, a 5-year-old boy with autism, is held by his father in Idlib, Syria, June 2022. © © 2022 Human Rights Watch. As armed conflicts proliferate around the globe, World Mental Health Day is a reminder that the psychological toll stemming from hostilities result in mental health harms that have lasting effects on people’s lives. Insecurity, trauma, anxiety, and confusion are the norm for many who have endured armed conflict. Access to services is frequently inadequate—even though over a fifth of conflict-affected populations are estimated to experience mental health conditions such as post-traumatic stress, depression or anxiety. For people, including children, with intellectual disabilities, these harms can be compounded by social, attitudinal, and environmental barriers, which interact with their disability and can heighten their exposure to violence and exclusion. The father of a boy with an intellectual disability in Syria, described in 2020 the effects that the war there had had on his son. The boy, who was 13 at the time, had become increasingly withdrawn and isolated. “He sits alone, doesn’t want to interact with any other kids,” said his father, who also described the psychological distress affecting his other children. “You can see the fear in their eyes. They have no hopes for the future.” Because of communication barriers, a lack of accessible information, and inadequate communication support, people with intellectual and other disabilities are frequently excluded from humanitarian assistance and mental health services, even when such services are available to others affected by the conflict. Human Rights Watch has documented lack of inclusive psychological support for people with disabilities in other armed conflicts, including Gaza and Sudan. Governments should address these gaps by integrating disability-inclusive mental health support during conflict and recovery, in line with their international obligations. Humanitarian agencies providing such services should also take steps to ensure that their programs are disability-inclusive and do not exclude people with disabilities. This could include providing accessible communication methods, such as pictograms and play therapy for children, training staff to provide disability-inclusive support, and equipping them with tactile regulation tools—like weighted lap pads, squeeze balls, and noise-canceling headphones—to help manage sensory overload. Accessible, inclusive mental health care and support are policies that cannot undo the trauma of war, but they can help create the conditions for recovery, inclusion, and hope for the future.

US Sanctions on ICC Put Global Justice at Risk. Click to expand Image Permanent premises of the International Criminal Court in The Hague, the Netherlands. © 2019 Peter Dejong/AP (New York) – The Trump administration’s decision to sanction the International Criminal Court (ICC) is an unprecedented assault on global justice and the rule of law, Human Rights Watch said today. On October 9, 2026, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the imposition of sanctions on the ICC. “The Trump administration has made clear its aim to destroy the ICC to shield US and Israeli officials from facing charges before the court,” said Philippe Bolopion, executive director of Human Rights Watch. “By attacking the court, the US government is threatening justice for victims of abuses from Palestine to Ukraine, Myanmar, and Sudan.” The ICC is a permanent international court created to try people, including senior officials, accused of war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide, and the crime of aggression. Following the genocides in the mid-1990s in Rwanda and in the former Yugoslavia, the international community created the ICC to prevent those most responsible for serious crimes from evading justice. Nearly two-thirds of UN member countries have joined the court. In addition to its Palestine investigation, the court has opened investigations into alleged crimes in 17 situations, including in Afghanistan, Darfur in Sudan, Bangladesh/Myanmar, Ukraine, and Venezuela. The US government’s decision to sanction the ICC was announced on the same day that the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge and renowned international lawyer, in recognition of her central role “in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.” In his October 9 announcement, Rubio stated the sanctions were aimed at shielding US nationals from investigation and prosecution at the ICC. The Trump administration has previously objected to the court’s investigation of Israeli nationals for their conduct in Palestine. The ICC has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for serious crimes in Gaza. Palestine became an ICC member in 2015 and gave the court a mandate to address serious crimes committed on its territory or by its nationals since June 13, 2014. The Trump administration has already sanctioned ICC prosecutors, nine ICC judges, three prominent Palestinian human rights groups, and the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, and called on ICC member countries to leave the court. US sanctions have serious effects on those targeted, including frozen or closed bank accounts, rejected financial transactions, denied access to digital services, and US entry bans. US sanctions also have a chilling effect on non-US banks and other companies outside of US jurisdiction that could themselves lose access to the US banking system if they do not adhere to the sanctions. This means that the ICC could lose access to companies on which it relies for everyday functions, from banking to information, technology to travel. Human Rights Watch, together with three other human rights organizations, filed a lawsuit in US federal court on August 11, 2026, seeking to have the sanctions regime previously used to authorize court-wide sanctions struck down. A wide range of human rights organizations, other experts, and former US government officials have filed amicus (friend of the court) briefs in support of the suit. ICC member countries, including the Netherlands which hosts the ICC in The Hague, the leadership body of the court’s Assembly of States Parties, the European Union, UN human rights experts, the UN secretary-general, the UN high commissioner for human rights, civil society organizations, and the ICC itself have repeatedly spoken out against the sanctions. The ICC and its member countries have also taken important steps to insulate the court from the potential impact of sanctions, but more action is needed to protect the court’s ability to continue its critical work. The EU should immediately activate its blocking statute, which aims to shield European operators from the effects of extraterritorial sanctions. The Trump administration’s sanctions targeting international justice are part of a broader attack on the laws, institutions, and organizations created to protect human rights, Human Rights Watch said. The United States has also withdrawn from the Paris Climate Accords and the World Health Organization, while disengaging from the UN Human Rights Council. President Donald Trump and other senior US officials have also expressed contempt for international law, and threatened to commit war crimes. “The ICC was created to ensure that no one, no matter how powerful, can escape justice for the worst crimes,” Bolopion said. “Governments everywhere should take every available measure to counter the effects of the US sanctions and stand with the court and those relying on it to obtain justice.”

Gaza: Ceasefire Anniversary Marks Year of Failed Promises. Click to expand Image A Palestinian boy walks inside a destroyed building in Khan Yunis in the southern Gaza Strip, January 27, 2026. © 2026 Bashar Taleb/AFP via Getty Images (Beirut) – Israeli forces continue to kill and wound civilians and deny sufficient food, aid, and water to Palestinians in Gaza one year after a ceasefire agreement took effect on October 10, 2025, Human Rights Watch said today. Israel’s acts of genocide and crimes against humanity, including forced displacement and extermination, have persisted throughout the ceasefire. Other countries should take immediate measures to protect civilians and ensure that rights-based reconstruction begins. The Board of Peace, authorized under United Nations Security Council Resolution 2803, is tasked with assessing parties’ compliance with the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict. Promises of humanitarian relief and the restoration of essential civilian infrastructure are central to the plan. Yet, a year on, aid volumes remain far below required levels, critical humanitarian access routes have been repeatedly obstructed, and reconstruction has not yet begun. Continuing Israeli attacks have killed at least 1,400 Palestinians and wounded 4,881 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry, bringing the death toll since October 2023 to over 74,000, including over 21,000 children. “The outside world may be under a dangerous illusion that life in Gaza is returning to normal, but reality tells a very different story,” said Sarah Sanbar, acting Israel and Palestine researcher at Human Rights Watch. “There is nothing normal about living in a tent under bombardment, without enough food or drinking water for your family.” With winter approaching, families living in an Israel-engineered shelter crisis face preventable deaths and suffering affecting key human rights such as the rights to housing, health, and education. Ninety-four percent of Gaza’s population lacks adequate shelter, the Palestine Shelter Cluster reported based on a survey of nearly 2,000 households across Gaza. Nearly two-thirds of housing units have been destroyed, and many of those still standing are damaged and unsafe. The survey showed that over half of the nearly 2,000 households are living in tents. In September 2026, a damaged building housing about 100 people collapsed, killing 21, including 12 children. Gaza’s education and health sectors remain shattered. The new academic year began last month with 93 percent of schools destroyed or damaged. The World Health Organization (WHO) recorded 56 attacks on health care in Gaza between January and August 2026, with just 35 of Gaza’s 57 hospitals and field hospitals partially functional and not one fully operational. Meanwhile, humanitarian organizations report an increase in disease due to the living conditions in overcrowded camps and shelters, including poor waste management, sewage overflow, and rodent infestation. The risks of famine and acute food insecurity loom over Gaza, as the entry of humanitarian aid remains limited and inconsistent, and people in Gaza are unable to produce their own food due to Israeli forces’ widespread destruction of agricultural land and restrictions on fishing. In July, the Integrated Phase Classification (IPC), the world’s foremost experts on food security, reported that 67 percent of the population—over 1.4 million people—are “expected to face crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity in July-December 2026.” According to the European Union and UN, the recovery and reconstruction needs in Gaza are estimated at US$71.4 billion over the next decade. On September 23, the Board of Peace presented a “6-Month Gaza Recovery Program” ready to begin “the moment funding and access allow,” but one year on, no recovery efforts have begun. Israel continues to move the “Yellow Line,” the stated limit of the physical presence of Israeli ground forces under the ceasefire, westward beyond its agreed boundaries as Israeli officials call the line Israel’s “new border.” The area within the Yellow Line now amounts to about 64 percent of the Gaza Strip, and Israeli forces are displacing Palestinians as the line moves while preventing residents from returning to their homes beyond the line, corralling Gaza’s 2.1 million people into an ever-shrinking strip of land. In June, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) documented that 196 Palestinians had been killed near the Yellow Line and its westward movement is swallowing up water points and health facilities, further restricting Palestinians’ access to key services. Alongside these actions, Israeli officials continue to openly declare a goal of ethnically cleansing Gaza. For example, in September, Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir proposed the “710 Disengagement Plan,” aiming to depopulate Gaza in seven years, and establishing a ministry of “voluntary emigration” for that purpose. According to Palestinian civil defense authorities, over 630 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble since November 2025, and they estimate that over 8,000 remain buried under the rubble. The UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory warned in September 2026 that the large-scale removal of rubble in areas of Gaza under Israeli military control should not become a way to erase traces of atrocity crimes. Finding the remains of those lost under the rubble is essential so that families can know what happened to their loved ones, offer them dignified burial, and start a long process of recovery and remedy, Human Rights Watch said. As world leaders discuss the future of Gaza, it is essential for them to urgently address the rights of Palestinians to rebuild their lives in Gaza, categorically reject all Israeli propositions of forced displacement and ethnic cleansing, and support all measures of accountability to put an end to the catastrophic situation for rights in Gaza. “Palestinians deserve a better future where their rights are respected and they can live in dignity, but none of this is possible unless the atrocities stop and justice and redress become a reality,” Sanbar said.

UN: Burundi Set to Win Human Rights Council Seat Despite Abuses. Click to expand Image Burundi's President Evariste Ndayishimiye speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, in New York, New York, September 23, 2026. © 2026 AP Photo/Heather Khalifa (New York) – Burundi is set to win re-election to the United Nations Human Rights Council in a vote on October 13, 2026, with no competition, Human Rights Watch said today. Burundi is seeking to retain its seat even though the government of this Central African country has not improved its abusive human rights conditions. Burundi is one of the four African countries running for the same number of seats on the 47-nation council. The regional slates for the Western group, Latin America and the Caribbean, Central and Eastern Europe, and Asia also lack competition. This effectively guarantees all 15 candidates, fit or unfit, spots on the UN’s premier rights body for three years beginning on January 1, 2027. “This uncompetitive vote makes a mockery of the word ‘election,’” said Louis Charbonneau, UN director at Human Rights Watch. “UN member states should insist on competitive slates so they can reject candidates with poor human rights records. No one should have a seat on this crucial body handed to them on a silver platter.” Ghana, Nigeria, and Zambia are candidates for Africa’s other three available seats. In Asia, Japan, Jordan, Kuwait, and Nepal are running for the region’s four seats. In Latin America and the Caribbean, Brazil, the Dominican Republic, and Uruguay are set to take the region’s three spots. For the Western group, Germany and Ireland are on track to get the group’s two available seats, while Moldova and Ukraine will take Central and Eastern Europe’s two spots. Despite some positive government statements, Burundi has not carried out meaningful reform to address longstanding concerns related to governance, justice, or accountability. Grave abuses persist with impunity, including extrajudicial executions, enforced disappearances, arbitrary arrests, and detention. Freedom of expression, assembly, and association remain severely restricted. Burundi is in the third year of its current term and is allowed to run for another consecutive term. On October 6, the country’s delegation tried to use their membership to prevent UN scrutiny of Burundi’s poor human rights record, first by calling a vote to renew the mandate of the UN special rapporteur on Burundi and then by voting against it. The resolution was adopted, though, 22 to 7, with 17 abstentions. That resolution not only expressed concerns about ongoing rights violations but highlighted Burundi’s refusal to cooperate with the council and most of its mechanisms, including the special rapporteur. General Assembly Resolution 60/251, which created the Human Rights Council in 2006, says that countries voting for members should “take into account the contribution of candidates to the promotion and protection of human rights.” Council members are required to “uphold the highest standards in the promotion and protection of human rights” at home and abroad and to “fully cooperate with the Council.” Candidates only need a simple majority in the secret-ballot vote in the 193-nation General Assembly to secure a seat on the Human Rights Council. That makes it highly unlikely that any candidate will lose, no matter how unqualified. Nevertheless, UN member states should not cast votes for abusive governments that are demonstrably unqualified for council membership. Among the other candidates, Nigeria should ensure accountability for serious international crimes committed by all parties—including security forces—during the conflict with the armed group Boko Haram. Brazil should investigate and curb police abuse after law enforcement officers set a grim record in 2025 by killing more than 6,500 people, the vast majority of them Black. Ukraine has suffered countless atrocities committed by Russian forces on its territory since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. At the same time, Ukrainian authorities have unjustly prosecuted Ukrainian civilians living under Russian occupation, including teachers, medics, municipal workers, and volunteers for doing essential work that international humanitarian law permits civilians to perform under occupation. The Human Rights Council scrutinizes all UN member states’ rights records in the Universal Periodic Review process. In November 2025, the United States refused to participate in its review. If the US government does not participate in its rescheduled review in November, it will become the first member country not to complete its review. The Human Rights Council has played a crucial role in ensuring independent investigations of abuses in Syria, Myanmar, North Korea, Russia, Ukraine, Israel/Palestine, Afghanistan, Sudan, and elsewhere. Council members should press for investigations of abuses by other countries in need of scrutiny, including major powers. These should include China’s crimes against humanity against Uyghurs and others in Xinjiang, as well as the US military’s unlawful strikes targeting vessels the Caribbean and Pacific, amounting to extrajudicial killings. The council should also explore possible action to support global justice in the face of a US assault on international accountability mechanisms. The US on October 9 imposed unjustified sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC). The Trump administration has made clear its aim to destroy the ICC to shield US and Israeli officials from facing charges before the court. The US had previously sanctioned ICC officials, Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on human rights in the Palestinian Territory occupied since 1967, and several prominent Palestinian human rights groups. “The human rights movement is under increasing attack by powerful governments, including established democracies,” Charbonneau said. “The Human Rights Council has done victims of human rights abuses a huge service with investigations that often deter governments and armed groups from committing violations. We need the council now more than ever.”

Senegal: Brutal Crackdown Violates LGBT People’s Rights. Click to expand Image Renovated Dakar Railway station inaugurated, May 2026. © 2026 Human Rights Watch Senegal’s intensifying crackdown on LGBT people is violating their rights and causing increasing fear and stigma. Fear of arrest and stigma are causing people to go into hiding, to avoid HIV testing and treatment, and deterring lawyers from representing them. The crackdown on LGBT people calls into question Senegal’s compliance with its own laws and international law, as well as the Olympic charter, given it will host the Youth Olympics Games at the end of the month. (Dakar) Senegal’s growing crackdown on Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender (LGBT) people is violating their rights, causing increasing fear and stigma, and should be ended immediately, Human Rights Watch said today. Mass arrests forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation appear to be part of an increase in punitive government action against LGBT people in West Africa. On March 11, 2026, Senegal’s parliament amended article 319 of the penal code, doubling to 10 years the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex conduct and criminalizing “promotion” of or support to LGBT people and organizations. The amendment followed the detention by security forces of at least five men in Thiès region in December 2025 and 12 men in the capital, Dakar, in February 2026 on charges including “acts against nature” and “intentional transmission of HIV.” Police and gendarmerie then escalated arrests of suspected LGBT people in various other cities including Thiès, Rosso, Saint Louis, Yeumbeul, and Ziguinchor. “LGBT people are being forced to curb their normal activities and to keep from exercising their rights for fear of arrest and increased stigma,” said Larissa Kojoué, LGBT rights researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Senegal’s government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone’s rights.” Human Rights Watch interviewed 39 people in May in Senegal: 5 people who had been detained in late 2025 and early 2026, 2 journalists, 9 civil society representatives and human rights defenders, 2 national officials, 2 lawyers, 4 health professionals, and 15 members of the Senegalese queer community. Human Rights Watch also reviewed official statements, and media and nongovernmental group reports. On September 29, Human Rights Watch wrote to the Senegalese authorities, including the justice minister, the high commander of the National Gendarmerie and director of military justice, and the director general of the National Police detailing its findings and asking specific questions, but has received no response. Same-sex sexual conduct has been criminalized in Senegal since 1965, but hostility toward LGBT people has significantly intensified in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, President Diomaye Faye and former Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko pledged to strengthen laws criminalizing same-sex relations, framing the issue as a national priority and mobilizing broad political and public support. The March amendments have triggered new attacks against LGBT people, interviewees said. Mouhamadou Seck, secretary-general of the prominent Senegalese organization African Forum for the Defense of Human Rights (Rencontre Africaine pour la Défense des Droits de l’Homme, or RADDHO), said in May that “detentions, violence, and abuse against LGBT individuals have sharply increased across the country.” Human Rights Watch was not able to independently verify the total number of arrests linked to article 319. However, between February and July, at least 212 people have been arrested, according to data collected by RADDHO. HIV Justice Network reported that the number of arrests exceeded more than 300 during the same period. Of those arrested, 82 were also charged with “voluntary HIV transmission,” although a court dismissed these charges in August. These figures illustrate the scale of arrests and indicate a pattern in enforcement of article 319. Security force officials have stated that they have arrested people suspected of engaging in same-sex conduct based on information extracted from previously seized phones, third-party allegations, or raids on private premises. The March amendment to the penal code introduces broadly defined offenses criminalizing activities such as “promotion” and “glorification” of homosexuality, as well as financing and supporting LGBT individuals and organizations. Human rights defenders and lawyers said that the introduction of these offenses has led to fear and anxiety among legal professionals and contributed to an environment in which detainees struggle to secure legal representation. “In Senegal, lawyers are associated with the cause they represent,” a lawyer in Dakar told Human Rights Watch, adding that his colleagues and family members had urged him not to represent individuals arrested on charges of “acts against nature.” He said: “Everyone has the right to a fair trial. What matters to me is: were their rights respected or not?” Principle 18 of the United Nations Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers provides that “Lawyers shall not be identified with their clients or their clients’ causes as a result of discharging their functions.” People interviewed said that since February, the authorities have subjected detainees to HIV testing without informed consent and used detainees’ HIV status to justify additional criminal charges or prolonged detention. Health professionals expressed concern that the forced HIV testing and subsequent charges undermine medical confidentiality by allowing confidential test results to be used in criminal proceedings. They also discourage people from seeking HIV testing and treatment and jeopardize HIV-related public health efforts. “We have noticed that […] some people have fled while others are hiding,” a doctor in Dakar said. “One-third no longer come in for appointments to seek HIV treatment.” Security forces also appear to have violated the confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBT people. News reporting on two cases involving public figures includes personal details that closely track details set forth in investigative records, suggesting authorities leaked confidential information to journalists. Local media also extensively reported personal and confidential data on the case of the 12 men arrested in February. This has exposed individuals to social stigma, family rejection, threats, and violence. The Senegalese Constitution and international human rights law applicable in Senegal guarantee fundamental rights, including equal protection before the law and non-discrimination; the right to effective legal representation and the presumption of innocence; the rights to privacy and to informed consent to medical treatment; freedom from torture and other ill-treatment, and the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time. Senegal’s Law No. 2010-03 of April 9, 2010, on HIV/AIDS establishes a legal framework to ensure access to treatment and support and protect the rights of people living with or affected by HIV. The law guarantees the rights to informed consent in medical testing and to privacy and confidentiality of health information, as well as protection against discrimination based on HIV status and protection of detainees from mandatory HIV testing. The African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, ratified by Senegal in 1982, guarantees, among other rights, the right to a fair trial, to equal protection before the law, and to nondiscrimination. The African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights, which will meet in Dakar from October 12–21, explicitly called on member states, including Senegal, to protect sexual minorities in accordance with the African charter, and has urged governments to protect people from violence based on their sexual orientation and gender identity. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), to which Senegal is a party, requires Senegal to ensure the protection of numerous rights including fair trial, equal protection, nondiscrimination, and the right to privacy. The UN Human Rights Committee, which oversees compliance with the ICCPR, has repeatedly held that the criminalization of consensual same-sex conduct between adults violates the covenant. From October 31 to November 13, Senegal will host the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, the first Olympic event on the African continent. The Olympic Charter prohibits discrimination on any grounds and commits host countries to respect human rights and human dignity. “The ongoing government crackdown on LGBT people raises serious concerns about Senegal’s compliance with international law, the Olympic charter, and Senegal’s own laws,” Kojoué said. “The government should call a halt to this crackdown.” Click to expand Image Interview with Sall (pseudonym), university student in Dakar, Senegal, who has barely left his room since February due to stigma and fear of arrest, May 2026. © 2026 Human Rights Watch Expanded Criminalization of Same-Sex Conduct On March 11, Senegal’s Parliament adopted amendments to article 319 of the penal code by a vote of 135 to 0, with three abstentions. The new law doubles, to 10 years, the maximum prison term for same-sex conduct and increases fines from 2 million to 10 million CFA francs (roughly US$3,000 to US$17,000). The law introduces penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5 million CFA ($850 to $8,500) for those accused of promoting homosexuality or supporting or financing LGBT persons and organizations. It also instructs judges not to suspend sentences or reduce prison terms below the minimum penalty recommended. Arbitrary Arrest, Detention According to data from July by the HIV Justice Network, since early February, authorities “have arrested over 300 individuals on allegations of acts against nature” in cities across Senegal. Data collected by RADDHO shows 212 people were arrested between February and July. RADDHO told Human Rights Watch that their data indicates that gendarmes from the Keur Massar unit carried out the majority of the arrests. Keur Massar is about 25 kilometers east of downtown Dakar. On June 25, Keur Massar district gendarmerie arrested the 101st suspect in connection with the arrest wave that began in February, according to media reports. Officers said the arrests followed their review of a mobile phone seized from one of the 12 men arrested in February. In July 30, international media reported that Keur Massar gendarmes arrested eight women who have been placed in pretrial detention. The gendarmes used phone data from two who were allegedly in a relationship to identify and arrest the six others. Beside “acts against nature,” investigators also cited allegations of pimping, corruption of minors, and drug-related offenses. Police in the Thiès region, about 70 km east of Dakar, arrested five men in December 2025 for smoking shisha, a tobacco product banned under local law, and held them for two days before presenting them to a judicial authority. The prosecutor ordered them held on charges of “acts against nature” but dropped the charges and released them a month later for lack of evidence. They said that they believe neighbors denounced them to the authorities because of their sexual orientation. One of the five, a 23-year-old man, said: We were arrested while preparing for a fashion show at my place. Around 9 p.m., three police officers arrived, took us to the station and confiscated our phones.… We were held for two days, then taken to the Thiès prosecutor’s office and charged with acts against nature, despite not being caught in the act.… I think our neighbors told the police we are gay because they were jealous of our successful fashion business. He said that, “we were beaten, whipped, and slapped, and called homosexuals.... I was injured on my thigh, causing lasting pain.” A social worker operating in Rebeuss, Senegal’s largest detention facility, located in Dakar, said he witnessed prison staff and detainees discriminate against those held on suspicion of homosexuality: “[LGBT detainees] are being excluded from communal activities, denied participation in collective prayer sessions, and required to access services, including the barber, separately from other prisoners. In some cases, they are even compelled to perform domestic labor.” Prolonged Pretrial Detention Since February, only one person arrested for “acts against nature” has been convicted according to local media. On April 10, the Pikine-Guédiawaye District Court, in a suburb of Dakar, sentenced a 24-year-old man, who had been arrested a week earlier, to six years in prison and imposed a fine of 2 million CFA franc (approximately $3,300) after convicting him of “acts against nature” and “public indecency.” He was not represented by legal counsel as it is often the case for people accused of “acts against nature” who may be denied access to legal representation or face difficulty finding lawyers willing to represent them. A lawyer in Dakar told Human Rights Watch that many of those arrested on homosexuality-related charges remain in pretrial detention because prosecutors have added supplementary charges, including criminal association, endangering the life of others, deliberate HIV transmission, and drug trafficking. The lawyer said that these additional charges often require longer investigations and are used to justify extending pretrial detention. Senegalese law generally limits pretrial detention to six months for minor offenses, with no limit for certain serious crimes such as murder, offenses against state security, and embezzlement of public funds.
